Jù (qí nì qiè). Yì (yīn yì). Wéirán (shàng: yǐ shuǐ qiè; meaning "yes" or "so be it"). Zhōngyāo (shàng: qù; xià: yú zhào qiè). Kù (kǔ wò qiè).
The Ritual for Repentance at the Amitābha Practice Hall, Scroll Two:
Resolving Doubts and Generating Faith, Part Two. (Alas!

Sentient beings have many doubts and meager learning; their obstructions are heavy and their merit is slight. Without texts that provide guidance, how could they understand the method for seeking rebirth? Now, therefore, questions and answers are provisionally employed, and host and guest are temporarily established, in order to resolve their state of doubt and cause them to generate faith.)
[Listen with] sincere faith).
Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment has already completed its refuge in the Triple Gem of the Western Quarter.

Next, we shall resolve doubts and give rise to faith. For the sake of all sentient beings, there have been various kinds of doubts within each person’s mind from beginningless time until now. Regarding these...
Because they are unwilling to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, or even if they desire to seek it, they do not know the Dharma gates;

instead, they mostly cultivate miscellaneous wholesome deeds that result in the impure, flowery rewards of humans and devas. Thus, they do not escape saṃsāra and undergo birth and death with immeasurable suffering and affliction.
For these fourfold assemblies, I have now selected various doubts of sentient beings from among the holy teachings and explained each one individually.
The *Shuchao* (Commentary) praises this, saying: "As for the cause, one practices for only one day or seven days; as for the fruit, one eternally attains *avaivartika* [non-retrogression].

Such a realm is startling to the ears and eyes. If it were during the Buddha’s lifetime or within the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), sentient beings would have superior merit, and their faith and wisdom would be profound;
hearing the Buddha speak once, they would believe with certainty and without doubt. Yet, how can it be so in the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma?"
Because their merit and fortune are inferior and their faith and wisdom shallow, upon hearing such a teaching, they immediately give rise to doubt and slander.

Therefore, when Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, preached this sutra, there were ten Buddhas, Tathāgatas, from each of the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of ten Gaṅgā rivers—who manifested great supernatural transformations.
I utter these words of solemn truth to testify that what my World-Honored One has taught is not erroneous.

Yet, from this day forward, there will be those without faith who, upon hearing of the practice of the Western Pure Land, will dismiss it as heterodox and incur the transgression of slandering the Dharma. How can they not fear?
All disciples of the Triple Gem ought to faithfully believe the words of the Buddha, just as a minister must trust the commands of his sovereign, or a son must trust the instructions of his father.
If one does not believe them, how can such a person be called a loyal minister or a filial son?
If those of the fourfold assembly take the Buddha as their teacher yet do not believe the Buddha’s words, they are not disciples of the Buddha; they are instead subjects of Māra.
Such persons are truly to be feared. That sentient beings are unable to have deep faith in the words of the sutras and harbor such doubts is entirely due to the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because they falsely give rise to inverted views and because of their doubt and confusion, they fall into the three [evil realms].
In the evil realms, what avail would repentance be? The great assembly should rely upon the Buddha’s words and practice according to his teachings without harboring any doubt.
If we do not repent and eliminate all our doubts and heavy karmic obstacles from the beginningless past until now, [they will remain].

There is no way to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Each person should, as if their head were on fire, seek mercy through prostrations and repentance, swiftly purifying uncommitted sins and vowing never to commit them again.
With a sincere mind, let us together cast our bodies to the ground in five-limbed prostration and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher;
homage to Lokeśvararāja Buddha; homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter;
homage to the Buddhas numbering as many kotis as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers.
Homage to all Buddhas of the present in the eastern direction.
Homage to Akṣobhya Buddha. Homage to Śailadhvaja Buddha.
Homage to Mahāśaila Buddha. Homage to Śailaprabha Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Subhaketu and to all such Buddhas as these, who dwell in the eastern direction in numbers like the sands of the Ganges River. From their own pure buddha-fields,
each manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm and surrounding it on all sides, as they proclaim the words of truth.
He said: "All you sentient beings should with faith accept this Dharma-gate of inconceivable praise for the merits of the Buddha-fields, which is embraced by all Buddhas."
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean.
Furthermore, take refuge once more in all the Three Jewels and immeasurable worthies and sages throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space (one prostration).

Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment should apply their minds with diligence; listen attentively with focused ears, so that the obstacles of doubt may be eliminated.
May body and mind be liberated; may I vow to leave the three miserable realms and seek rebirth in the nine grades of the Pure Land.

Past births and deaths are as immeasurable as the kalpa-stone; future cycles of saṃsāra are as endless as a mustard-seed city. I only pray that with the three minds I shall rouse my resolve and through ten recitations achieve success.

Once the conditions for birth in this world have ceased, the wondrous realm of that land will immediately appear. Supported from behind by auspicious clouds and welcomed from before by pure companions, in a single kṣaṇa—

One attains rebirth immediately; for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one shall eternally dwell in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Now, having resolved doubts and given rise to faith, [the author] sets forth the explanation in sequence, asking:
"The *Chengzan shu* (Commentary on the Praise) says: 'How is it that by reciting with the mouth and contemplating with the mind, one immediately attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land?
The answer is: The mind takes the Buddha’s realm as its object, remembering and upholding it without forgetting; the mouth recites the Buddha’s name."
It is clear and undisturbed. In this way, mind and speech, internal and external, correspond with one another.

If one recites even a single phrase of "Namo Amitābha Buddha," it can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas and accomplish the sublime merit of eighty billion kalpas.
If even a single phrase is thus effective, how much more so ten phrases, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand?

In this manner, throughout one day, one month, one year, or an entire lifetime—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—if one practices with diligent effort day and night, what sins and defilements would not be eliminated?
What merits would not increase? For what reason would one not be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? By what cause would one fail to behold Amitābha Buddha?
It is like an infant who, when struck by fear, cries out and calls for its parents;

moved by compassion upon hearing their child's cry, the parents set aside all other affairs and hasten to rescue and protect them. So it is with the sentient beings of this present age of the five turbidities.
Constantly oppressed by the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and the three miserable realms, once they have become aware of this, they immediately give rise to alarm and fear.
With a sincere mind, they loudly invoke the name of that Buddha to seek protection.

Amitābha Buddha possesses the supernormal power of the divine ear and will certainly see them from afar; he possesses the supernormal power of the divine mind and will certainly know of them from afar. Thus, the Buddha—
Compassion differs from the deluded affection found among humans; [the Buddha] regards all sentient beings as equal to his own children.
He will certainly come in person to bestow compassion and guide us. This is because the power of the vows of Amitāyus Buddha in the Western Quarter is profound and heavy;
he constantly uses his radiant light and sacred name to gather and transform sentient beings. We, the children of the Buddha, having now [been joined] with the Buddha...
This accords with the Original Vow; the principle must necessarily be so. Do not give rise to doubt or hesitation.

If sentient beings, with a heart of sincere resolve, recite the name for one thought-moment, ten thought-moments, one day, or seven days, they shall all attain rebirth by virtue of the Buddha’s power of the vow.

Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice should arouse a mind of valor, a mind of profound reverence, a mind of sincere devotion, a mind of firm resolve, and a mind of non-retrogression.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher;
homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter; homage to Maitreya Buddha of the Future;
homage to the Buddha Vīradatta; homage to the Buddha Viśuddha.
Homage to the Buddha Viśuddhadatta. Homage to the Buddha Śālendrarāja.
Homage to the Buddha Varuṇadeva. Homage to the Buddha Dṛḍhaśrī.
Homage to the Buddha Candanaguṇa. Homage to the Buddha Amitaketurāja.
Homage to the Buddha Prabhāśrī. Homage to the Buddha Aśokaśrī.
Homage to the Buddha Nārāyaṇa. Homage to the Buddha Guṇakusuma.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva;
homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean.
Furthermore, I take refuge in all the Triple Gem and the immeasurable worthies and sages throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space.

(One prostration). He asked: "The *Jueyi ji* states: 'If one merely perceives one's nature and awakens to the Way, one transcends birth and death; why then is it necessary to fixate the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in his land?
Answer: The minds of others—whether sages or ordinary beings—are obscured and unfathomable; this cannot be known through anything other than the Right Universal Wisdom (*samyak-sarvajñāna*)."
It would be difficult to grant such a prediction [of enlightenment]. A true practitioner should examine themselves: as when a person drinks water, they know for themselves whether it is cold or warm.

You, virtuous ones, should observe your own conduct and understanding; upon seeing your nature and awakening to the Way, you shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeed to the rank of the Patriarchs.
To be able to possess unimpeded eloquence like that of Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, and to realize the three periods of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—to be thus...

The Tiantai Master Zhiyi did not exclusively follow one school of teaching, but rather practiced all paths while maintaining a comprehensive understanding; he was able to do so like National Teacher Huizhong and Chan Master Shou.

These various great beings all clearly transmitted their verbal teachings and earnestly exhorted others toward rebirth in the Pure Land. This is truly for the sake of benefiting both oneself and others.
How could one dare to mislead others and oneself? Moreover, the Great Hero has offered praise and the golden mouth has issued earnest exhortations;

following the examples of past sages and reverently receiving the Buddha’s decree, this is certainly not erroneous. Furthermore, you should reflect for yourself upon the moment of death, when life and death part ways and one must depart.
One will certainly attain mastery. One’s own heavy karmic obstacles from beginningless time will certainly not manifest.

Not merely liberated from saṃsāra through this single retribution-body, one will be able to dwell at will throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether in the heavens or among humans—certainly without hindrance.
If one can thus clearly and personally realize this with confidence, what excellence could surpass it? If this is not yet the case, [one must strive further].
Do not, out of temporary arrogance, cause yourself to fall into eternal samsara; do not lose your own opportunity for wholesome benefit—whom else would you blame?
Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now? An ancient worthy said: "Though conditioned phenomena are false, if one abandons them, merit and practice will not be accomplished.
Though unconditioned reality is true, if one merely pursues it, the fruit of sainthood is difficult to attain. To awaken to the Way in a single kṣaṇa requires long-term cultivation.
"Smelted and refined through kalpas; sudden enlightenment of the one mind must necessarily rely upon the perfect cultivation of the myriad practices. How true these words are!
Yet today, the indolent followers of this degenerate age have little learning but many doubts; they recklessly indulge in arbitrary speculations, misleading themselves and others.
Truly, they are those who deserve pity.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, with one mind and sincerity, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
Homage to the Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha!
Namo to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter. Namo to Maitreya Buddha of the Future.
Namo to Padmaprabha-vikrīḍita-ṛddhi Buddha.
Namo to Dhanaśrī Buddha. Namo to Śrīkūṭa Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha of Virtuous Renown and Merit. Homage to the Buddha King of the Crimson Flame Banner.
Homage to the Buddha of the Merit of Wandering Steps. Homage to the Buddha of the Jewel Flower Wandering Steps.
Homage to the Buddha King of the Sāla Tree, Well-Abiding upon a Jewel Lotus.
Homage to the Buddha Victorious in Battle. Homage to the Buddha Skillful Gait.
Homage to the Buddha Adorned with Merit on All Sides.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean.
Furthermore, I take refuge in all the Triple Gem and immeasurable worthies and sages throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space.
(One prostration).
He asked: "Since all ten directions are pure lands, why do you point specifically to the west?
He replied: "Because the power of the Master’s vow is supreme, and all sutras collectively extol and recommend it."

(*The Treatise on the Ten Doubts*, Fascicle 4, states: Question: Since the practice of *nien-fo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) is the same when seeking rebirth in the pure land of a single Buddha, why not recite the name of any one Buddha among those of the ten directions?

Why is it necessary to focus specifically on Amitābha Buddha of the West? Answer: Ordinary beings lack wisdom and do not dare to act arbitrarily; rather, they follow the words of the Buddha. Therefore, they focus specifically on Amitābha Buddha. How do they follow the Buddha’s words?

It is because throughout the holy teachings of Śākyamuni Master’s entire life, he repeatedly exhorted sentient beings to single-mindedly and specifically recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. As seen in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-kalpa-sūtra* and other texts, through seventy-six kinds of causes and conditions, he earnestly instructed them to seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.)

Regarding the Buddha-fields: although other Buddhas’ various pure lands are briefly recommended for rebirth in one or two sutras, none compare to the Land of Amitābha Buddha, which is recommended for rebirth throughout numerous sutras and treatises. This is why one should focus one’s mindfulness exclusively upon it. As the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows* states:

The Bodhisattva Puguang asked the Buddha, “World-Honored One, there are pure lands in all ten directions; why do you specifically praise the Western Pure Land of Amitābha and exclusively dispatch beings to be reborn there? The Buddha told Puguang, “The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have minds that are mostly turbid and distracted.

For this reason, I specifically praise the pure land of a single Buddha in the West, so that these sentient beings may concentrate their minds on a single object and easily attain rebirth. If one were to mindfully recollect all Buddhas, the scope of the mindfulness would be vast, and the mind would become scattered.”

[Objection: Samādhi is difficult to achieve; therefore, one cannot attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Furthermore, the merit of one Buddha is no different from the merit of all Buddhas, because they share the same Buddha-nature (*dharmatā*).

For this reason, to recollect Amitābha Buddha is to recollect all Buddhas; to be born in one Pure Land is to be born in all Pure Lands. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The bodies of all Buddhas are the body of a single Buddha; likewise, their single mind, single wisdom, power, and fearlessness are also so. It further says:

Just as the pure full moon universally reflects in all waters, though its reflections are infinite, the original moon has never become two; so too, the one who has attained perfect enlightenment through unimpeded wisdom manifests Buddhas in all lands, yet his body is not dual.
Question: I doubt that my own past karma is heavy, while the merit of ten recitations is slight.
Answer: A thousand years’ growth of ten thousand trees / Is turned to ash by a single fire.

(The *Ten Doubts Treatise*, Chapter Eight. Question: Since beginningless time, sentient beings have created immeasurable karma. In this present life, having received a single form, they do not encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and further commit every kind of transgression, leaving no evil undone. How can this be at the moment of death?)

If one achieves ten recitations, one immediately attains rebirth, transcending the matters of karmic bondage within the three realms. How can this be reconciled? The answer is: since beginningless time, sentient beings have been unable to know the quantity or the strength of their seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma.

If one is able to encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the moment of death and achieve the ten recitations, it is entirely due to the power of strong past wholesome karma that one first encounters such a virtuous friend and achieves the ten recitations.

If one’s evil karma is heavy, one will not even be able to meet a virtuous friend; how then can one discuss the achievement of the ten recitations? Furthermore, regarding your claim that beginningless evil karma is heavy while the ten recitations are light, I shall now use three principles to weigh their relative gravity:

it is not fixed by time, duration, or quantity. What are these three? First, that which resides in the mind; second, that which resides in the conditions; and third, that which resides in determination. Regarding that which resides in the mind: when committing a transgression, it arises from one's own false delusions; whereas mindfulness of the Buddha arises from the wholesome.

Regarding knowledge: when one hears the true merits and the name of Amitābha Buddha, how can a state born of the unreal be compared to one born of the real? It is like a dark room ten thousand years old where the light of the sun briefly arrives and the darkness is instantly extinguished;

how could it be said that the long-standing darkness cannot be dispelled? As for the conditions: at the time of committing transgressions, one follows the delusive darkness of falsehood, with the mind conditioned by unreality and perceptions turned upside down.

Yet, upon hearing the pure and true merits and name of the Buddha, and being conditioned by the unsurpassed bodhicitta, a state of the truly real arises. How can the one that is false be compared to the one that is authentic? It is like a person struck by a poisoned arrow—the shaft deep and the venom cruel, wounding the flesh and breaking the bone—yet as soon as they hear of the medicinal drum that eliminates it, [the pain is gone].

The arrow will then emerge and the poison be removed. How could one refuse to extract it simply because the arrow is deep and the poison is virulent? Regarding the state of certainty: at the time of committing a transgression, there is an interrupted mind and a subsequent mind; at the time of recollecting the Buddha, there is an uninterrupted mind.

There was no subsequent thought, and he immediately passed away. Because his wholesome mind was so intense and sharp, he was reborn at once. It is like a rope ten spans thick that a thousand men cannot restrain, yet a youth brandishing a sword divides it in two in an instant. Or like a pile of firewood accumulated for a thousand years that is consumed by a single bean-sized spark, which is exhausted in a brief moment.

Furthermore, it is like a person who has cultivated the ten wholesome deeds throughout their entire life and ought to be reborn in heaven, yet at the moment of death gives rise to a single thought of wrong view and immediately falls into the Avīci Hell.

Since even a false and deluded evil karma, when it is so intense, can displace a lifetime’s worth of wholesome karma and cause one to fall into the evil realms, how much more so when, at the moment of death, one recollects the Buddha with a fierce mind, truly and without interruption? Wholesome karma cannot displace such beginningless evil karma. One attains [rebirth].

It is impossible that one would not be born in the Pure Land. Furthermore, it is said: "Reciting the Buddha’s name for even a single thought-moment extinguishes the sins of birth and death committed over eighty billion kalpas.

Because the mind is sharp and intense at the time of reciting the Buddha’s name, evil karma is suppressed and extinguished; one will certainly attain birth [in the Pure Land], so there is no need for doubt. Regarding the ancient tradition that judges ten recitations as being accomplished only at another time, this is certainly untenable. Moreover, the *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* states:

A king asked the śramaṇa Nāgasena, "If a person in this world commits evil for a hundred years, yet recites the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, they will be born in the Buddha-land after passing away. I do not believe these words. Nāgasena replied: "It is like placing a hundred large stones on a boat; because of the boat, they do not sink. Although..."

Originally evil, yet by reciting the Buddha's name for even a single moment, one does not enter the hells. As for those whose names were omitted from the boat, it was because they committed evil and did not know to recite the Buddha’s name, whereby they entered the hells; how could there be any doubt in this?
Question: How can ordinary beings bound by all fetters be born in that pond?
Answer: Through their own power over many kalpas; through the Buddha’s majestic power in a mere instant.

(From the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, Chapter Five. Question: Ordinary beings bound by all fetters have heavy and thick evil karma and all afflictions; not even a hair’s breadth has been severed. The Western Pure Land transcends the three realms. How can such ordinary beings bound by all fetters attain birth there? Answer:)

It is said: There are two kinds of conditions: first, self-power; second, other-power. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In this world, there are two ways to cultivate the path: first, the difficult path; second, the easy path. As for the difficult path, it exists within the evil world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

To seek *avaivartika* [non-retrogression] during the time of immeasurable Buddhas is extremely difficult to attain. These difficulties are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be fully described; here, I shall briefly state five of them. First, the similar goodness of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) which confuses the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.

Second, unscrupulous and wicked people who destroy the supreme virtues of others. Third, perverted wholesome fruits that can ruin pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Fourth, the self-interest of the Śrāvakas which obstructs great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Fifth..."

There is only the power of self, without the support of another's power. It is like a lame person walking on foot; in one day they can travel no more than a few *li*, undergoing extreme hardship—this is called the power of self. As for the path of ease, it means to believe in the Buddha’s teachings, practice the *nien-fo* samādhi, and vow to be born in the Pure Land.

By being sustained by the power of Amitābha’s vows, one will certainly attain birth. This is like a person traveling by water; because they rely on the power of a boat, they reach a distance of thousands or tens of thousands of *li* in a mere moment—this is called the power of another.

If one says that an ordinary person bound by all fetters cannot attain birth, this is equivalent to the analogy of the lame person. The treatise further states: "When an inferior man follows a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), he travels around the four continents in a single day; this is not his own power, but the power of the Wheel-Turning King. Now, [the text] cites the power of self.

With the faith of the mind, one boards the teaching-ship of Śākyamuni; unfurls the light sail of skillful means; secures the upright rudder of diligence; follows the path guided by the assembly of sages; rides upon the wind of Amitābha’s vow-power;
and drifts upon the dharma-stream of the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi to reach the other shore of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Question: The pleasures of the celestial palaces are not few; why is it necessary to earnestly exhort one to go to the West? Answer:
There are the five signs of decline and the ten inferiorities; these are not for long-lasting duration. (The *Cien Tongzan* states: Question:

The bliss in Maitreya’s celestial palace is no small matter, and excellent companions are many there. Why is it necessary to earnestly exhort one to be reborn in the Western Land? Answer: If one speaks of Tuṣita, it indeed surpasses the human realm, yet it is still on par with the West.)

[The latter] is entirely inferior. Since the superior and the inferior differ, each side is distinct. To "exhort one to be born in the Western Land" means to abandon the inferior and seek the superior. Regarding the difference between the superior and the inferior: there are ten excellences of the Pure Land and ten deficiencies of the celestial palaces. As for the ten excellences of the Pure Land:

The ten superiorities of the Buddha-land: first, superiority in the excellence of the abode of the Transformation Lord; second, superiority in the longevity of those to be transformed; third, superiority in the non-affiliation with the realms of existence; fourth, superiority in being a pure region free from desire; fifth, superiority in the absence of female inhabitants; sixth, superiority in the non-retrogression of practice; seventh, superiority in being a pure region rather than a defiled one; eighth, superiority in the adornment of the land;

ninth, superiority in the gathering of the emotions through mindfulness of the Buddha; tenth, superiority in rebirth through ten recitations. The ten inferiorities of the celestial palaces: first, inferiority in the land where they reside; second, inferiority in the brevity of the lifespan of those to be transformed; third, inferiority in being bound and subject to the realms of existence;

fourth, inferiority in having desire within those heavens; fifth, inferiority in the mixed residence of men and women; sixth, inferiority in the occurrence of retrogression in practice; seventh, inferiority in being a defiled region rather than a pure one; eighth, inferiority in the adornment of the land; ninth, inferiority in the gathering of the emotions through wholesome thoughts; tenth, [inferiority in the lack of rebirth].

The hardships of their practice are inferior; furthermore, although their lifespan is four thousand years, when their own lives are about to end, five signs of decline appear: first, the flowers upon their heads wither; second, filth exudes from beneath their armpits; third, they become unstable in rising and sitting;

fourth, their physical strength and vigor decay; and fifth, they are subject to much agitation. Because there are these ten inferiorities and five signs of decline, [the Buddha] encourages one to be born in that land. Again, it was asked: "The wondrous pleasures of the devas and their long lifespans spanning many kalpas—"

One is fully capable of practicing the Way; by accumulating merit among humans, one may likewise transcend even the three miserable realms of asuras, nāgas, and ghosts. This is precisely how one may uproot suffering and benefit sentient beings—why then must one single-mindedly strive only for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? The answer is as follows:

The various devas of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are addicted to exquisite pleasures and intoxicated by the wine of heedlessness; they forget the west while looking toward the east, and among those who are greedily deluded and dissolute, there are many, while those who resolve their minds to cultivate goodness are few.

When their merit is exhausted, they fall like an arrow shot into the air. Although the devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) move alone without sexual union, they have not yet exhausted the burden of physical form. The devas of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) likewise do not escape saṃsāra; the sutras judge these realms to be "difficult grounds. Master Fu said: "Even if one passes through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end, this is but falling into emptiness and oblivion.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the ten classes of immortals each attain a mode of existence and live for millions of years, dwelling in deep mountains or on islands in the great ocean far from the haunts of men; yet when their retribution is exhausted, they return and are scattered into the various realms of rebirth. Only the Pure Land is an exception.

The companions of this one gate are sages and worthies who, in a single kṣaṇa, transcend the three realms; because they dwell in constant bliss, it is said that the land is superior to being bound by the realms (from the *Jizhao ji*).
Question: It is said that taking birth in Tuṣita is excellent; within the inner court, there is no returning [to saṃsāra]. Answer: Who is like Siṃhabuddhi?
Even in the outer court, one still remains steeped in delusion. (The *Ten Doubts*, Fascicle 7, states: Question:

Maitreya Bodhisattva is in his final birth before Buddhahood and will immediately attain enlightenment. Those who practice the ten wholesome deeds of the highest grade can be born there and see Maitreya Bodhisattva. Why, then, must one seek birth in the Western Land? Answer:)

It is said: Seeking rebirth in Tuṣita may seem similar in principle, yet when compared, there is a great difference in their relative merits. First, let us discuss two points. First, even if one were to maintain the ten wholesome precepts, there is still fear that one might not attain rebirth. How is this known?

The *Maitreya’s Ascent Sūtra* states that one must practice various samādhis and enter deeply into right concentration (*samāpatti*) before one can begin to attain rebirth; it offers no further means of being guided or received. This is unlike the power of Amitābha’s original vows and the power of his light, which simply embrace and do not abandon any sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Second, just as during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha there were many sentient beings who saw the Buddha yet did not attain the fruits of sainthood—being as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—so too will it be when Maitreya appears in the world. There will likewise be a great many who do not attain the fruits of sainthood. Not yet...

In the Pure Land of Amitābha, once one has been born in that land, all have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and not a single person has ever fallen back into the triple world to be bound by the karma of birth and death.

Furthermore, I have heard a tradition from the Western Regions stating that there were three bodhisattvas who cultivated the Tuṣita heaven: the first was named Asaṅga, the second Vasubandhu, and the third Siṃhabuddhi. They made an agreement that whoever was first born into Tuṣita and saw Maitreya should come and inform the others. Siṃhabuddhi died first, yet for several years there was no report.

Next, Vasubandhu died, and after three years, a report finally arrived, saying: "The days in the celestial palace are long. I have been born in Tuṣita, where I pay homage to Maitreya Buddha and listen to his preaching of the Dharma; I have already been here informing you for three years. When they asked about Siṃhabuddhi, he replied: [The response follows: "He is currently serving as a gatekeeper at the entrance to the palace."

Those born in the outer court of Tuṣita are attached to celestial pleasures and thus never see the Buddha; they merely cultivate Tuṣita as Bodhisattvas while still harboring such attachments. This failure to see the Buddha is the very root of saṃsāra. Thus we know that cultivation in Tuṣita is difficult and prone to downfall, unlike the West (Sukhāvatī), where cultivation is easy and free from downfall.

Furthermore, the *Bailian ji* (White Lotus Collection), in the fourth section on "Praise, Censure, and Doubt regarding the Former Master," asks: "The Dharma Master Ci'en was counted among the thousand Buddhas; he composed a commentary on the *Sutra of Rebirth Above* and offered praises [to Amitābha]."

The Inner Court (Neyuan) said: "There are seven changes in being born in the celestial palaces, while there are ten difficulties in being born in the Pure Land. Since what the Venerable Master taught must not mislead people, I do not yet understand how these two views are to be reconciled.

He replied: "You know only the *Commentary on the Sutra of the Ascent to Heaven* (Shangsheng shu) by Ci'en; you do not know his *General Praise Commentary* (Tongzan shu). That *General Praise Commentary* states that the Pure Land has ten excellences while the celestial palaces have ten deficiencies, and it instead exhorts people to seek birth in the Pure Land. How could the Venerable Master’s compositions be mutually contradictory? It is simply because he expounded the teachings according to the capacities of beings, showing different expedient means for each.

What difference is there in intent between this and the World-Honored One’s own preaching in the *Amitābha Sūtra* and other texts, which exhorts birth in the Western Land, versus his preaching of the *Sutra of the Ascent to Heaven*, which exhorts birth in the Inner Court? Sentient beings differ in their karmic conditions."

The Buddha-lands that are embraced are also diverse. For example, suppose there is a person whose circumstances lead him to the south; he intends to travel to Wu and Yue by boat, so he prepares his gear and inquires about the route.

When a wise man responds to his inquiry, how could he instead praise the convenience of land travel or extol the advantages of Qin and Shu? To do so would only increase confusion and bring no benefit. Those who are versatile and far-sighted know where to turn according to their aspirations, whereas those of shallow views and doubt stubbornly create contradictions.

This is like the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*) being held in high esteem by the world, yet becoming a poisonous drug when encountered by such people. I universally exhort future generations: do not peer at the sky through a tube, nor measure the ocean with a ladle; do not harbor doubts or slander regarding the Buddha-lands, lest you bind yourselves with the causes of suffering. Be deeply cautioned! Be deeply cautioned! Furthermore—

The *Nianfo Sanmei Yi* (Ritual for the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) by the Grand Master Sikong states: Emperor Xingzong personally inscribed a question, asking: "Should ordinary people of the present age seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss?

I, being honored to respond, said: "A person dwelling in this floating world is like a traveler lodging in a guest house. Even if one were to live out a full hundred years, it would still be like the passing of a single instant. The faculties are dusted with the external defilements of the six sense objects, and consciousness is scorched within by the three fires. Moreover, there is no substantial pleasure to be craved; even if there were empty splendors, what would one have to cling to?

For this reason, the sages of the West and the philosophers of the East followed one another’s footsteps, examining their lives and wearying of abiding in the mundane realm, while in every thought they rejoiced in approaching the Buddha-realm. Some prayed upward to Maitreya, vowing to go to the celestial palace; others prayed westward to Amitābha, seeking rebirth therein."

The Pure Lands are all swift paths for transcending the mundane and essential gateways for entering the state of sainthood. If discussed in terms of those external realms, they appear differently in each location, with both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) manifesting together. Alternatively, if distinguished from the perspective of one's own mind, the two meanings differ in their explanation.

Both ease and difficulty are present here. It is not that Tuṣita is exclusively a land of transformation and thus easy, nor that the Pure Land is exclusively a land of retribution and thus difficult. This is because the *Tuṣita Sūtra* states that great bodhisattvas from other directions come to the assembly and reside within the celestial crown.

If one wishes to seek rebirth in the Transformation Tuṣita Heaven, there are seven easinesses (*sukha*). If one wishes to seek rebirth in the Retribution Tuṣita Heaven, it possesses many difficulties. This is because the Tuṣita Heaven encompasses both retribution and transformation;

thus, for those seeking rebirth there, there are both ease and difficulty. The Western Pure Land also has two kinds: first, the Transformation Pure Land, as the sūtras permit the birth of ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*); second, the Retribution Pure Land, as the śāstras state that women and followers of the Two Vehicles do not exist there.

If one wishes to seek rebirth in the Pure Land of the Retribution Buddha, according to the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Rebirth Above*, there are ten difficulties. If one wishes to seek rebirth in the Pure Land of the Transformation Buddha, according to the teachings of various sūtras, there are likewise ten easinesses: 1. Because Amitābha’s vows are weighty, rebirth is easily attained (as stated in various sūtras). 2. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss... [text continues]

1. It is easy to attain rebirth without opposition. (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*) 2. It is easy to be sustained by the Buddhas of the thirty directions. (*Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*) 3. It is easy for a single Buddha of the east to assist in one's accomplishment. (*Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra*) 4.

It is easy for two great sages to come and welcome one. (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*) 5. It is easy for eight great bodhisattvas to lead one away. (*Also from the Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*) 6. It is easy to attain rebirth by practicing the ten vows. (*Avataṃsaka Sūtra, "Chapter on the Practice of Vows")* 7. It is easy to attain rebirth by copying a single sutra. (*Sūtra of the Decisive Radiance*) 8.

It is easy to attain rebirth by dedicating miscellaneous merits. (*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*) 9. It is easy to attain rebirth by recollecting the Buddha for a short time. (*Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Infinite Life*) Because the supreme teachings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are universally communicated and transformed, seek them.

Birth may be easy or difficult. Now, Your Majesty the Emperor, having been born among humans and attained the position of sovereign, can verify your past causes through the fruits of this present life. You must have already once resolved upon the Great Bodhicitta; you must have already once cultivated the practices of the Great Bodhisattvas.

Although external circumstances were powerful and your own will was lax, causing occasional lapses, your faith was compelling and your resolve firm, such that in every thought-moment you constantly contemplated what is virtuous and beneficial. In your youth, you already partially received the Bodhisattva precepts; this year, you again fully received the Upavāsa (Eightfold) precepts.

Furthermore, you constantly recollect the Eight Bodhisattvas and perpetually maintain a heart of Great Compassion. Moreover, you have extensively performed acts of merit in various places—constructing temples and copying scriptures, providing vegetarian feasts for the Sangha, and creating blessings. If one seeks only the retribution of birth as a Buddha...

The Pure Land is indeed difficult to attain. However, if one simply seeks rebirth in the Transformation Land (nirmāṇakṣetra) of the West, aspiring to behold the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of Amitāyus Buddha, this is highly consistent with principle and does not exceed one’s capacity.

According to the sutras and commentaries, if one receives the Buddha-precepts and for a period of one day up to seven days performs these acts—making offerings to the Buddha, providing meals for the Sangha, erecting stupas and building temples, copying sutras and crafting images, reciting the names of the eight Bodhisattvas, and maintaining the Great Compassion Mantra—and then dedicates these merits toward rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, all of these goals will be attained.

One will be reborn there according to one's wish. Upon being born, one will immediately behold Amitāyus Buddha and the eight bodhisattvas. One shall never again regress from the unsurpassed path, nor fall once more into the three evil realms.

All sufferings and afflictions therein are entirely absent; its wealth, nobility, and adornments are beyond description. I pray only that you maintain single-minded faith and diligent practice, and do not harbor doubts or vacillate between advancing and retreating. (All other ordinary people should understand this by analogy.)
Question: Regarding Maitreya’s assembly under the Dragon-Flower Tree, even when that appointed time arrives, one still departs [from saṃsāra].
Answer: In five million six hundred thousand years, the final descent will still be delayed.

(*Nienfo jing*). Question: When Maitreya descends in the future, he will preach the Dharma in three assemblies to deliver all sentient beings, enabling them to attain the fruit of Arhatship. Why, then, do you not vow to be born there? Why instead seek birth in the Pure Land of Amitābha?

The answer is: Until Maitreya descends to be born, it is impossible to wait for him. How is this known? It is stated in the *Ūrdhvasūtra* that five billion six hundred and seventy million years will pass after Śākyamuni Buddha enters parinirvāṇa.

Only then will he descend to be born here. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Descent* states that Maitreya shall appear only when the waters of the ocean have receded to three thousand *yojanas*. According to the *Record of the Original Account of the Dharma King*, more than two thousand years have passed since the *parinirvāṇa* of Śākyamuni;

it is not yet time for him to come. One must not wait for him, for the lives of sentient beings are short; one fears sinking into the sea of suffering and undergoing calamity for many kalpas without encountering Maitreya. Now, Amitābha Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma, dwelling in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), extensively delivering sentient beings.
They took refuge in the Western Quarter and early on realized the fruits of the Path.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, with one mind and sincerity, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Question: To loathe suffering and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—how can this be considered having compassion?
Answer: If one wishes to treat the illnesses of others, one must first heal oneself.

(The *Ten Doubts Treatise*, Fascicle One, states: Question: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their vocation. If they wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings, they should simply vow to be born within the triple world to save suffering beings amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable realms.)

"Why seek rebirth in the Pure Land to settle oneself while abandoning sentient beings? This would be a lack of great compassion, dedicated solely to self-benefit, and an obstruction to the path to Bodhi. Tiantai Zhiyi replied: "There are two kinds of bodhisattvas.

The first are those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); they are indeed the ones who deserve such reproach. The second are those who have not yet attained [this stage] and have returned [to the world], as well as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have first resolved their minds on enlightenment.

As for these ordinary bodhisattvas, they must always remain inseparable from the Buddha and achieve the power of patience before they are fit to dwell within the triple world and rescue suffering sentient beings amidst evil ages. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: 'It is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters to possess a heart of great compassion and vow to be born in an evil age to rescue suffering sentient beings.'"

This is the case. Why is this? In an evil world, afflictions are naturally powerful and one lacks the power of forbearance. The mind turns according to external objects, bound by sounds and forms, and thus one falls into the three miserable realms (trāya) of one’s own accord.

Even if one could rescue sentient beings and happen to be born among humans—becoming a king, a high minister, or enjoying wealth, nobility, and autonomy—even if such a person encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they refuse to trust or follow their guidance. Greed, delusion, and negligence lead them to commit a multitude of transgressions. Driven by these evil karmas, they enter the three miserable realms and remain there for immeasurable kalpas.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the body of a lowly and wretched being; yet if they do not encounter a spiritual friend, they fall back into hell. Such is the cycle of saṃsāra that persists to this day. Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "If one cannot even save oneself when ill, how can one save those who are sick? Furthermore, it says:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For example, suppose there are two men, each with relatives who have been swept away by water. One man, driven by urgency, plunges straight into the water to rescue them; however, lacking skillful means (*upāya*), both he and his relatives drown. The other man possesses skillful means;

he goes to fetch a boat or raft and rescues them by means of it, so that all are freed from the peril of drowning. A bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] is likewise: as long as they have not attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*), they cannot save sentient beings. For this reason, they must always remain close to the Buddha.
Only after attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can they save sentient beings, just like the one who obtained the boat."
Question: When the Buddha appears at the moment of death, how can one distinguish between what is false and what is true?
Answer: The celestial Māras dare not appear; this is the Buddha—cease further doubt. (The *Bailian ji* states: Question:

When auspicious signs appear, their nature is uncertain; they may be either false or true. At the time of death, how can one discern them? If one does not recognize them, how can one choose which to accept or reject? Answer: Recite the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth.)

Such persons receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas; therefore, Māras do not dare to manifest. Even if they do manifest, it is certainly within the realm of the Buddhas. The *Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas* states:

"If there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus and, with single-minded faith and joy, uphold, recite, and contemplate it, such persons shall obtain immeasurable merit and shall forever remain far removed from the calamities of the three miserable realms. At the time of their death, if they maintain single-minded faith and joy, contemplating [the Buddha] without forgetting or abandoning him, Amitābha Buddha will lead a multitude of bhikṣus to appear before them.

Māras can ultimately never destroy the right-enlightenment mind of such individuals. Why is this? Because that World-Honored One has given rise to great compassion, vowing to deliver all immeasurable sentient beings, and he likewise protects them."
(Question: "If immeasurable people are to be transformed, how can Amitābha know them all?
(Answer: "It is like the moon dwelling in the void; everywhere it receives its radiance."

(Longsu Wen said: Question: "When those who practice with diligence reach the time of their death, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to welcome them. Now, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable sentient beings who are diligent; can the Buddhas know all their appointed times and go to welcome them all? Answer:

"The Buddha-body is like the moon, its reflection appearing in all waters. When the water is clear, the reflection appears; thus, there is no sequence of coming or going. Therefore, the ancients said: 'The Sage of Great Vows comes from the Pure Land—yet in coming, there is truly no coming.

The ordinary person of deep resolve goes to the Pure Land—yet in going, there is truly no going. He does not come here, nor do you go there, yet the ordinary and the sage meet, and both achieve communion. Amitābha’s radiance is like the great full moon, appearing everywhere throughout the ten directions.'"")

When water is clear and still, the moon manifests its true form; yet the moon does not hasten to the water to come there. When water is turbid and moving, the moon lacks a fixed radiance; yet the moon does not abandon the water to depart in haste. It is within the water that there is clarity or turbidity, stillness or movement.
In the moon, there is no grasping or rejecting, no coming or going).
Question: "Ten million billion lands to the west—the road is so far that I fear it will be difficult to return.
Answer: "If the soul can travel ten thousand li in a dream, how much more so when relying on the Buddha’s majestic power?"

(The *Ten Doubts Treatise*, Fascicle 9, states: Question: The Western Land is ten thousand billion Buddha-fields away from here. Since ordinary people are physically frail and weak, how can they possibly arrive there? Answer: This is spoken merely in reference to the physical eye of ordinary beings and the mental capacity of those within the cycle of birth and death.

Although the Western Land is ten thousand billion Buddha-fields away, for any sentient being who has perfected the karma for the Pure Land, the concentrated mind at the moment of death is itself the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land. A single movement of thought brings one to birth in the Pure Land; therefore, the *Contemplation Sutra* says, "The land of Amitābha Buddha is not far from here.

Furthermore, the power of karma is inconceivable: in a single thought-moment, one is born there. There is no need to worry about the distance. It is like a dream: although the body remains on the bed, the mind, intellect, and consciousness travel everywhere.)

Furthermore, all worlds remain no different than they were before. Birth in the Pure Land is likewise so; it arises the moment a thought is stirred—there is no need for doubt. Moreover, the *Amida Shō* (Commentary on Amida) addresses this: Question: The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that the Western Land is "not far.

Yet, the Western Land is ten thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-fields away from here. Why, then, is it said to be "not far"? Answer: There are two meanings. First, "not far" in terms of rebirth. The *Contemplation Sūtra* says: "In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, one attains rebirth in that land. Second, "not far" in terms of the welcoming descent. The Sūtra says:
"At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha and his assembly of holy beings appear before one. Furthermore, regarding distance and proximity, if one has faith, it is near; if one lacks faith, it is far.
Question: If one carries the debt of killing and the karma of enmity, how can one possibly escape it?
Answer: After being reborn and attaining Buddhahood, one will deliver them together;

of this there is no doubt. (Longshu Wen says: Question: A person who has committed evil throughout their life, harming sentient beings and causing suffering to the people, may still attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death. However, those sentient beings who were killed or harmed harbor feelings of grievance and injustice.)

"When can one be liberated? He replied: "After being born in the Pure Land and attaining the Way, one is able to deliver all enemies and kin. Is this not far superior to those who harbor resentment and seek retribution from their enemies, for whom there is no end in sight?"
Question: If one attains rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death, why is it necessary to practice and cultivate superior deeds in advance?
Answer: Human life varies in its duration—some die young and others live long. It is difficult to foresee whether one will encounter one of the ten types of untimely death;

perhaps one will suddenly fall ill, become exhausted, or lose consciousness. *The "Comprehensive Praise of Ci'en" states: Question: If performing virtuous acts at the time of death allows for rebirth, why must one cultivate various supreme deeds beforehand? Answer: Human life spans vary in length, making it impossible to predict their brevity or longevity. One might suddenly be stricken by illness, fall into a state of delirium, or...*

Thus, one may suddenly pass away at an untimely hour; having lacked the wholesome roots cultivated during life, it is difficult to escape the calamities of future rebirths. To prevent such faults, one should proactively establish conditions for merit. The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states that there are ten circumstances at the end of life when one is unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha:

first, one may not necessarily encounter a virtuous friend; second, one may be so entangled by illness and suffering that one has no leisure to mindfully recollect the Buddha; third, one may suffer from a stroke that causes loss of speech, making it impossible to invoke the Buddha’s name; fourth, one may become deranged and lose one's senses, making focused contemplation difficult to achieve; fifth, one may suddenly encounter water or fire, leaving no time for sincere resolve;

sixth, one may unexpectedly meet with beasts of prey such as jackals or wolves, finding no virtuous friend to assist; seventh, an evil friend may arrive at the moment of death and destroy one's faith; eighth, one may overeat until one falls into a stupor that leads to death; ninth, one may be engaged in military service; [and tenth, one may be caught in the midst of a great assembly].

In the midst of battle, one may suddenly fall into the cycle of rebirth; or perhaps one might abruptly tumble from a high cliff, injuring one’s body and ending one’s life. In such cases, one cannot wait until the moment of death to achieve the ten recitations.

(One prostration). Question:
When dwelling within the lotus bud, it is difficult to determine whether there is suffering or joy.
Answer: It is like being in the Yāma Heaven; the wondrous bliss is inconceivable.

(*The White Lotus Collection* says: Question: I do not yet understand whether one experiences suffering or pleasure within the flower. Answer: One’s dwelling place within the flower is like the pleasures experienced in the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens. Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, fascicle 18, states:

For example, just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, and others sport and enjoy themselves within palaces eight hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas in size, I see those in the world of Sukhāvatī who dwell in the womb as being like those in the Yāma Heaven abiding in their palaces.
Question: "The wise person knows that the mind is the Buddha; the foolish person loves to go to the West. Answer: "Roots and conditions vary in being sharp or dull;
the teaching is expounded according to each individual's capacity. (The *Jizhao ji* states: The question asks:

The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* says, 'Ordinary fools do not understand their own nature and do not recognize the true Buddha within their bodies. Those who wish for the West from the East, and those who wish for the East from the West—those who have attained awakening are of one kind wherever they may be. Master Zhiyi [Zhigong] said:...)

The wise know that the mind is the Buddha; the ignorant cherish the journey to the West. If this were truly the definitive Dharma-gate, why would the two Great Beings (Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra) have rejected it? The answer is: In the Buddha’s teaching, there is concealment and manifestation; in the instruction, there is the provisional and the ultimate.

Sentient beings have varying capacities—some sharp, some dull—and the Patriarchs employ methods of suppression and encouragement accordingly. It is like how illnesses differ, and thus prescriptions vary. Suppose there is a patient with fever and jaundice whose condition has become violently deranged;

a skilled physician will certainly treat them with cold-natured medicines. How could one then praise the efficacy of milk-stone, cassia, and cinnamon for removing cold and restoring health? If someone with biased views hears that cold-natured medicines can treat heat, they might conclude that milk-stone, cassia, and cinnamon can never be used. Is this not a grave error?

The Patriarch transmitted the mind-seal alone; Master Zhi praised the Great Vehicle as "directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. In this, both [subjective] Buddha and [objective] Dharma are absent, and no reliance is placed on words or letters. At that time, people had not yet accepted this; how could one further teach them to recite the Buddha’s name in order to seek rebirth?

Those with perfect faculties and penetrating understanding will naturally have no doubts. However, those who first seek the Dharma will certainly give rise to hesitation. Yet, if they grasp the meaning while forgetting the words and achieve a comprehensive, integrated understanding, there will naturally be no contradiction.
Question: "Non-conceptualization is nirvana; conceptualization is delusion. Answer:
"Who would harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s words that command us to dwell in the sixteen contemplations?

(The *Bailian ji* states: The question asks, "The *Pratyutpanna Sūtra* says: 'It is my own mind that creates the Buddha; it is my own mind that sees the Buddha. To have conceptual thoughts is delusion, while non-conceptualization is nirvana. Now, if one gives rise to thoughts to contemplate the Buddha, is this not delusion?")

The answer is: Capabilities differ and teachings vary; the intentions of the Sages are difficult to fathom. There are many gateways for negation and affirmation, and the textual meanings are not uniform. Sometimes negation is applied from the perspective of principle, while the mind follows along with conceptualization, yet neither constitutes an error. Alternatively, one may negate objects and apply antidotes; in this regard, one must clarify what constitutes opposition or conformity according to practice.

Conformity is the thought of pure goodness; opposition is the thought of defiled evil. If one contemplates purity with thoughts of goodness, then the realm of good manifests; if one contemplates defilement with thoughts of evil, then the realm of evil manifests.

Therefore, the *Vaipulya Bhadrapāla Sūtra* states: "If one has evil desires and thinks of a woman, one sees a woman in a dream; if one has wholesome desires and thinks of the Buddha, one sees the Buddha in a dream. This indicates that these two types of thoughts are distinct in name and substance, such that good and evil are worlds apart. One must not hear the term "thought" and indiscriminately loathe it all.

If one were to loathe it thus, they would oppose the Buddha and slander the Dharma. To oppose the Buddha is not to be a child of the Buddha; to slander the Dharma is to enter the hells of the ten directions. How can one not be cautious? Moreover, this practice of contemplation is the primary cause for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is the very source by which all ordinary beings become sages.
How could one treat the womb with such ease and fail to follow [the proper rites]?
Question: In the *Strīvivaraṇa* (Discourse on Women), it is said that birth in a lotus pond is not permitted.
Answer: As soon as one arrives at the lotus pond, one transforms from female to male.

(The *Bailian ji* says: Question: The treatises state that women, as well as those with impaired faculties, are not reborn there; how is this to be reconciled? Answer: Women in this realm who seek rebirth there will attain it; at the time of being born in that land, they are transformed into men.)
Question: There are also practitioners who do not delight in seeing Amitābha.
Answer: Because they lack the seeds of past affinity; because their obstructions are heavy, what doubt is there? (The *Bailian ji* says: Question:

Why is it that some people do not delight in being born in Sukhāvatī? Answer: Because they lack the seeds of past affinity; because they cling to views and engage in discrimination, they do not delight [in it].)
Question: Suppose one lacks faith and respect; what fault is there in slandering [the Buddha]? Answer:
One who obstructs others from seeking rebirth shall fall into the hells for many kalpas.

(The *Mahāyāna Repentance Ritual*, Volume Three, states: Question: Even if this were so, if one does not believe, what transgression is committed? Answer: The *Sūtra on Praising the Merits of All Buddhas* says: "If there are those who do not believe in the praise and extolling of Amitābha...")

Those who slander the merits of the Buddha’s name shall, at the end of their lives, fall into the Avīci Hell for a full five kalpas, where they will undergo all manner of suffering. Furthermore, they shall become hungry ghosts for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, and even animals for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, constantly being harmed by weapons and the like.
(From the *Chudizhao* [Excerpts on the Names]) Moreover, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states: "If there are people—whether men or women—who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and do not believe;

or those who do not believe the words of the sūtras, do not believe in the community of bhikṣus, and give rise to doubt, having no faith whatsoever—all such persons shall, because of these causes, come from the evil realms to be born in ignorance. They will not understand their past lives, and as their calamities and evils are not yet exhausted, they have not yet attained liberation. Thus it is said.

In my heart, I harbor doubts and do not yet believe this. Furthermore, the *Ganlu shu* (Commentary on the Nectar) states: According to verified accounts and oral traditions, during the Dali era, there was a man in Hengzhou named Zhang Yuan. Because he had slandered others, he fell ill and his body began to rot.

Every evening, he saw a Vajrapāṇi spirit, about thirty feet tall, cast into a great pit where it suffered extreme agony. After several weeks, the spirit let out a lowing like an ox and died with its tongue fallen out.

Zhang Yuan had several brothers who, because they delighted in his slanders, all likewise had their bodies rot and their tongues fall out before dying one after another. Instances such as these are very numerous and cannot be recounted in full; what is recorded in the scriptures and traditions is truly terrifying.

The Ritual for Repentance at the Meditation Hall of Amitābha, Scroll Three: Section Three, Citing Teachings and Corroborating with Evidence. (Now, as for citing teachings and corroborating with evidence:

one gathers the essential words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and selects from the writings of the various masters. Pruning away the redundant and the coarse, one extracts the refined essence. A single word of the direct path allows one to emerge from saṃsāra; the Dharma-gate of six characters enables one to transcend birth and death directly.)
It is only by relying upon the sacred teachings that one may avoid sinking into the depths of saṃsāra.
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice has already resolved their doubts and given rise to faith; their minds are now clear and relaxed, like ice melting away.
Now, once again, I shall cite the teachings as corroboration to sweep away any remaining delusions. Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, you have accumulated evil...
Like the sands of the Ganges, the sins committed fill the great earth; from casting off one body to receiving another, one neither perceives nor knows [the consequences].
Such various defilements of sin have causes and conditions that are immeasurable and boundless; today I confess them openly and pray that they may be extinguished.
The *Water Repentance* (Shuichan) states briefly: first, one should give rise to five kinds of mind as a preparatory means, and only then can these sins be extinguished.
What are these five? First, shame and remorse; second, fear and dread; third, weary detachment; fourth, equanimity toward enemies and kin;
and fifth, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses. Regarding the first, shame and remorse: one reflects, "I and Śākyamuni Tathāgata were once fellow ordinary beings.
Yet now, since the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, an incalculable number of kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges have already passed."
"Friends, we have together become addicted to the six sense objects and transmigrate through birth and death with no prospect of escape;
this is truly something for which we should feel shame and remorse in this world. As for the second terror:

since we are ordinary beings whose physical, verbal, and mental actions are constantly associated with transgressions, by reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of our lives, we shall fall into the three realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
They are smeared with the evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering; thus, this is truly something to be feared and terrified of. Third, as for wearying detachment:
one should constantly contemplate that within birth and death, it is like a turning wheel, where the eight sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death converge before one.
There is not a moment’s rest; this body is a collection of manifold sufferings, and everything within it is impure. What wise person would take pleasure in this body of birth and death?
Since it possesses all manner of evil dharmas, it is utterly loathsome and one should seek detachment from it. Fourth, regarding equanimity toward enemies and kin:
one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, free from the notions of "other" and "self. Why is this so?
If one perceives an enemy as distinct from a friend, this is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Because of such discrimination, one gives rise to hatred and attachment;

due to these conditions of aversion and compliance, one creates various evil karmas. When these evil karmas ripen, one reaps bitter fruits. When others come with hostility, one must respond with intimacy;
toward those who harbor venom, one should repay them with kindness. One should contemplate thus: "In the past, I troubled you, but now you..."
They are angry with me; this is due to my own past karma. Even if I were to lose my life, I would accept it with a willing heart, let alone their anger.

Even assuming that I committed no fault in a previous life, yet they now harbor resentment and malice toward me, treating me with unjust contempt and oppression, one should reflect: "That person is a wise one."
I wish to bring the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to fulfillment; such a person is my teacher. How could I encounter them otherwise? I should only look up to them in gratitude;
how would I dare harbor any resentment? If they lack wisdom, they are simply a field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*), like a mother who hears her child returning her insults.

The mother’s joy was redoubled; she merely continued to stroke him, never showing a trace of anger. Out of pity for his childish ignorance, she bestowed only deep kindness upon him. Now it is the same:
he is besieged within by afflictions that delude his very being, secretly causing his nature to become deranged and his strength to fail so that he lacks self-mastery.
With this compassionate heart, one should only extend rescue and salvation; how could it be right to dwell on his faults or consider him an enemy? If such thoughts were to arise...

If it contradicts one’s own mind, how does it differ from delusion? When people wish for something to be strong, they project strength upon it; when they wish for something to be high, they project height upon it.
How could there be any compliance or resistance, or hatred and love, within that? Thus, enemies and kin are equalized. Fifth, regarding the contemplation on the emptiness of the nature of offenses:
they have no substantial essence or characteristic; they arise from causes and conditions and exist through inversion. Since they arise from causes and conditions...
Thus they arise; thus, from causes and conditions, they cease. That which arises from causes and conditions is the cultivation of unwholesome deeds through associating with evil friends.
That which ceases from causes and conditions is precisely the purification of the mind and repentance performed today. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The nature of this transgression is neither within, nor without, nor in between. Therefore, one knows that this transgression originally arises from emptiness.
The six roots are fundamentally pure; the four great elements are originally empty. When both object and self have vanished, what is there to be called suffering?
To eliminate the root of delusion, one must perceive the spiritual source. Thus, realizing the emptiness of nature is the true extinction of transgressions.

"If one were to provide the four types of material offerings to all sentient beings and cause them all to attain the fruit of Arhatship, would their merit not be great?

Bhadrapāla replied, "World-Honored One, that merit would be exceedingly great. The Buddha told Bhadrapāla, "It would not equal the merit of someone who encourages another to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha even once; the latter surpasses the former. How much more so when considering oneself! If even a single recitation is thus, how much more so many? Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra* states:

"If the fourfold assembly were to take seven treasures filling the entire world and offer them as alms to all the Buddhas of the ten directions, it would not equal a person who, with a sincere heart, makes an offering of a single coin, a single incense stick, or a single flower to Amitābha Buddha. By performing this merit..."
As for "virtue," all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajra-devas, and others will be fully delighted; one shall die and be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

If a person lights lamps as an offering to Amitābha Buddha, at the end of their life they will be born in that Buddha-land and immediately attain the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), seeing clearly through to all worlds in the ten directions. The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra* states: "If..."
If a Wheel-Turning King, for a full hundred thousand years, were to bestow the seven treasures throughout the four continents as offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions,

and recollects the virtues of Amitābha Buddha until they are reborn in that land after death. As stated in the *Ānanda-yamukha-dhāraṇī Sūtra*:

At the time of their death, eight bodhisattvas will come riding upon supernormal powers to show them the way;
they shall then be spontaneously born within a precious lotus flower in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
