Regarding wholesome practices, there are differences in their relative difficulty. Those who cultivate other wholesome deeds in a general manner rely solely on their own power;

they must practice for many kalpas without regressing before they can attain the fruit of sainthood, which is therefore extremely difficult. However, those who recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land rely on the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows, which sustain and never abandon them;
thus, there is little risk of falling back, making this path exceedingly easy. It is, for example, like...
Both individuals desired to cross the sea to go to the Mountain of Jewels. One of them planted trees, intending to use them as a boat once they were grown;
however, this took a very long time, and due to many obstacles and difficulties, he was unable to cross.
Those who rely on their own strength to practice other virtues are also like this. The other person, meanwhile, encountered a great merchant leader on the seashore.
A great ship, with gentle words, addresses the great merchant leader: "Out of compassion, please grant me permission.

Immediately he boards the vessel, and before long, he reaches the place of jewels. It is the same for those who, relying on the power of Amitābha’s vows, maintain mindfulness of the Buddha and seek birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is said: "From immeasurable kalpas in the past until now, one has constantly experienced suffering and affliction; each and every..."
The skeletal remains accumulated by sentient beings within a single kalpa would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha;
the milk they have drunk would equal the waters of the four great oceans; the blood shed from their bodies would exceed the waters of the four great oceans;
and the tears shed from weeping for deceased parents would exceed the waters of the four seas. Thus they sink into the vastness of kalpas, failing to encounter a Buddha-King. And so it is.
The Buddha appeared in Śrāvastī in Central India, yet three hundred million people neither saw nor heard him; in one region of China, none knew or perceived it.

Those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties face heavy obstructions and find it hard to encounter him; Buddhas rarely appear in the world, and being in such hardships, one lacks the conditions to meet him.
Although one was born at a time when not meeting a Buddha, one nonetheless rejoices in encountering this sutra.
The Recorded Sayings and Dharma Teachings of Elder Jiaochang (Exhortatory Preface):

It is because those who first enter the Way have not yet purified their power of forbearance and must rely upon pure conditions as a superior support. Why is this? In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni has already passed into extinction and Maitreya has not yet been born.

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those two supreme beings personally serve as one’s excellent friends. In the Sahā world, various demons ultimately cause disturbances for the practitioner; in the Great Radiance of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is certainly no occurrence of demonic affairs. In the Sahā world, false sounds are chaotic and confusing.

The seductive charms of female beauty exist here; yet in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the waterfowl and the forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Their primary retribution is pure, and there are no actual women there. Thus, one may ask whether the conditions for cultivation are complete or not. If those in the West who possess only shallow faith give rise to groundless doubts and slanders, let me briefly discuss this:

among the people of this land, there are none who do not weary of the clamor and vexation of the secular home and yearn for the tranquility of the *araṇya* (forest hermitage). Therefore, when they abandon their homes to leave the household life, everyone praises them with great earnestness. Yet, what of the manifold sufferings of the Sahā world? They far exceed the mere clamor and vexation of a secular home.

And what of the leisurely ease of the Land of Ultimate Bliss? It is by no means merely the tranquility of a forest hermitage. To recognize the excellence of leaving the household life, yet to have no desire to be reborn in the West—this is the first delusion. To toil with hardship over ten thousand *li*, traveling afar in search of a spiritual teacher...

This is because [the Pure Land path] elucidates the Great Matter and resolves the questions of life and death; yet, the World-Honored One Amitābha’s physical and mental karma are supreme, and his power of aspiration is vast and profound—when he utters a single perfect sound, there is nothing it does not clearly harmonize with.

To wish to associate with spiritual friends while having no desire to see the Buddha is the second delusion. Monastic communities and large assemblies are all places where people delight in dwelling, yet one does not wish to rely upon them for a small-scale place of practice; yet in the World of Ultimate Bliss, those who are "one-life-to-enlightenment" (ekajātipratibaddha) are exceedingly numerous, and all the most virtuous beings assemble in one place.

To desire to frequent monastic communities while not admiring the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude is the third delusion. In this land, the maximum lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, and from childhood ignorance through senility, diseases follow one another in succession, accompanied by dullness and torpor.

Sleep occupies more than half of one's life. Even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "shading of the womb" (*yinye*), and Śrāvakas still lack clarity regarding their emergence from it. Thus, of every inch of jade and every moment of time, nine-tenths are lost; yet, without having attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), one may truly be said to have cause for heartache. This is the condition of people in the West.

Their lifespan is immeasurable. Once they have taken birth within a lotus calyx, they shall never again suffer the pain of death. They will continue in an uninterrupted succession until they reach Bodhi; thus, they immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), their progression toward Buddhahood becomes certain, and while the fleeting life in this Sahā world is subject to transmigration, here it is no longer so.

To remain deluded regarding the Pure Land for many years—this is the fourth error. Only when one’s rank is non-retrogressive and the fruit of realization is the birthlessness of *anutpāda*, such that one is free from desire while amidst desires and remains undefiled while dwelling in the dust of the world, can one truly give rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sahaja-karuṇā*).

Only then may one return to the toils of the mundane world, blending with the light within the five turbidities. Yet those who possess only shallow learning and solitary wisdom, or who merely correspond to a small measure of goodness, immediately claim to have transcended the four currents of existence and loftily surpassed the ten stages (*bhūmi*). They revile the Pure Land, cling to this Sahā world, and close their eyes to return to a void emptiness.

They wander aimlessly as if adrift, side by side with oxen and horses, following one another into the hells (*niraya*). Unaware of who they truly are, they compare themselves to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta; this is their fifth delusion. Thus, the Sūtra says: "One should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.

To fail to believe the sincere words of the Buddhas and not vow to be reborn in the Pure Land—is this not most profound ignorance? An ancient master said: "The single gate of Buddha-recitation possesses seven kinds of excellence: first, the excellence of having few words and being easy to practice; second, the excellence of taking the Buddha as the object of mindfulness."

3. The excellence of attaining peace by being free from calamities; 4. The excellence of extinguishing sins through the recitation of the name; 5. The excellence of obtaining merit through upholding and mindfulness; 6. The excellence of the fruition of seeing the Buddha; 7. The excellence of being personally welcomed to rebirth. These are the ten excellences of Amitābha. 1. The excellence of being able to fulfill all that is sought.

1. The excellence of meeting the two parents upon rebirth; 2. The excellence of being welcomed by light and transcending the world; 3. The excellence of attaining the Dharma upon hearing the name; 4. The excellence of transforming one's substance upon hearing the name; 5. The excellence of practicing with reverence upon hearing the name; 6. The excellence of realizing the fruit upon hearing the name; 7. The excellence of receiving a superior birth upon hearing the name;

8. The excellence of possessing virtues upon hearing the name; 9. The excellence of non-retrogression upon hearing the name. The Ten Excellences of the Pure Land: 1. The excellence of encountering the Triple Gem upon birth; 2. The excellence of swiftly attaining the supreme Dharma; 3. The excellence of obtaining a superior physical form upon birth;

4. The excellence of having no evil, only goodness; 5. The excellence of having no suffering, only pure bliss; 6. The excellence of obtaining all necessities according to thought; 7. The excellence of a long and far-reaching lifespan; 8. The excellence of non-retrogression in practice; 9. The excellence of a land that is not bound by realms; 10. The excellence of the adornments of the land. Rebirth.

Ten Superiorities: 1. The superiority of ease in rebirth as taught in the sutras; 2. The superiority of rebirth through even a brief period of cultivation; 3. The superiority of being protected and remembered by the assembly of sages; 4. The superiority of being embraced by the light [of Amitābha]; 5. The superiority of relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows; 6. The superiority of being personally welcomed by the Lord of Transformation (Amitābha);

7. The superiority of being witnessed and certified by all Buddhas; 8. The superiority of being able to extinguish all transgressions; 9. The superiority of being praised together in all the scriptures; 10. The superiority of proceeding alone when the Dharma has perished. Furthermore, ten easinesses for rebirth: 1. The easiness of rebirth through the arising of faith, understanding, and aspiration; 2. The easiness of rebirth through performing even a small amount of wholesome deeds;

3. The easiness of rebirth through practicing a single contemplation; 4. The easiness of rebirth through being embraced by the compassionate light and vows; 5. The easiness of rebirth through the praise and exhortation of various teachings; 6. The easiness of rebirth through the praise and exhortation of all Buddhas; 7. The easiness of rebirth through the empowerment and protection of the assembly of sages.

1. It is easy to attain birth [in the Pure Land]. 2. It is easy to attain birth through being gathered by the transformative power of the two sages. 3. It is easy to attain birth by recollecting [the Buddha], which extinguishes all transgressions. 4. It is easy to attain birth by being welcomed by the sages at the time of death.

(The *Bailian ji* states: The Layman of Mount Xiang, Bai Juyi, whose courtesy name was Lètián, composed the "Record of the Painting of the Western Paradise" and made this vow: "I, the disciple Bai Juyi, burn incense and prostrate myself, kneeling before the Buddha.

Arousing a heart of compassion, I make this great vow: May the merit of this act be transferred to all sentient beings. For those who are aged like me, and for those who are ill like me, may they all be freed from suffering and attain happiness; may they sever evil and cultivate goodness. Without even crossing the Southern Sea, may they behold the Western Paradise. )

The great light from the ūrṇā-kośa shall respond to one’s thoughts and manifest; through the highest grade of the blue lotus, one shall be reborn according to one’s vow. From this present body until the end of the future, may one always be able to draw near and make offerings. Desiring to proclaim this vow once more, he spoke these verses of praise:
[The Pure Land of Sukhāvatī is free from all evil realms and manifold sufferings; may those like this aged body afflicted by illness and pain be reborn together with the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
— Li Bái (Táng), Preface to the Dharma-Gate of Praise.

(*Báilán jí* states: Li Bái of the Táng dynasty, style name Tàibái, created a transformation tableau of the Western Pure Land using gold-paste paint, and wrote a preface stating: "To the west of our Buddha’s golden heaven, where the sun sets, lies a distance of ten trillion *kṣetra*s from the Middle Kingdom.")

There is a world called Sukhāvatī. The Buddha of that land is sixty million *yojanas* in height. The white tuft of hair between his eyebrows curls gracefully to the right, like five Mount Sumerus. His eyes are clear and white, like the waters of the four oceans. He sits upright preaching the Dharma, eternally and serenely present.

The ponds are bright with golden sand; their banks are lined with precious trees; jeweled nets cover everything; railings and curtains surround them; and carnelian and lapis lazuli adorn the towers and palaces, while beryl and agate illuminate the splendor of the steps and terraces. All these are realized by the Buddhas; they speak no falsehoods.

Whether one has already made the vow and seeks to attain it, or is currently making the vow, whether one has already been born there or is yet to be born—by focusing the mind with diligence for seven days, one will certainly be born in that land. The merit is boundless and manifest.

(Verse of Praise for the One Whose Name is Hard to Pronounce): Gazing afar toward the west, where the sun sets, I behold the countenance of Great Compassion. His eyes are as pure as the waters of the four oceans; his body’s radiance is like a mountain of purple gold. Through diligent practice, one will surely attain rebirth there; therefore, it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

With nets of pearls and trees of precious jewels, celestial flowers scatter upon fragrant pavilions. This scene is as clear as if painted before my very eyes; I vow to take refuge in that sacred field. By this ocean of merit, may you provide secret protection as a bridge and raft.
Sins of eighty billion kalpas Are swept away like wind dispersing light frost; May I behold Amitāyus And forever gaze upon the light of his jade-like brow.
The Layman Dongpo’s Verses on the Dharma Gates (*Bailian ji* states:
The Layman Dongpo, Su Shi, styled Zizhan, composed a hymn in praise of Amitābha, which says):

The Buddha, with Great Perfect Enlightenment, Pervades worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; I, through inverted thoughts, Arise and perish within birth and death. How can I, by means of a single thought, Attain rebirth in the Pure Land?

The karma I have created since beginningless time Originally arises from a single thought; Since it arises from a single thought, It likewise perishes from a single thought. In the place where arising and perishing are utterly extinguished, Then I and the Buddha are identical.
Like water cast into the sea, Or like bellows blown by the wind— Though there be the wisdom of a Great Sage, He could not distinguish them. May my deceased parents, Along with all sentient beings...
Wherever one dwells, it is the Western Land; Whatever is encountered is all Sukhāvatī. Every person is Amitāyus; There is neither going nor coming.
Preface and Praise for the Dharma Gate (from the *Jueyi ji*).

The "Unconditioned Son" (Wúwéizǐ), Yang Jie, style name Cìgōng, wrote a preface stating: In the *Avataṃsaka*, the Householder Vimukta says: "To know that all Buddhas are like reflections and one’s own mind is like water—those Tathāgatas do not come to [the mind]."

This is so. I do not go to that place; yet if I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Land of Peace and Bliss, it is accomplished simply by my will. Knowing that sentient beings fix their minds upon him, they will certainly see Amitābha, who will come to welcome them. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away—this is a statement of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), not a provisional teaching.

The Pure Land has no desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) pools of craving. Its land is situated in the physical world, not the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Those born there possess physical forms, not the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). All sentient beings have not yet awakened to perfect enlightenment; they dwell within a great dream, rising and sinking through the six realms of existence without ever ceasing.

Though the heavens are pleasant, when their retribution is exhausted, their appearance declines. The asuras are filled with rage as they wage war for victory. Animals fly and run about, devouring one another in mutual cruelty. The ghosts and spirits dwell in darkness...

Oppressed by the darkness of the realms, tormented by hunger and thirst, and wailing in pain throughout the long nights of hell, one may fortunately attain birth in the human realm. Yet, there one remains entangled in the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Only this Pure Land is free from all such suffering. Entrusting one’s essence to the womb of a lotus bud, there is no suffering of birth.

Cold and heat do not shift, so there is no suffering of old age. One’s lifespan is immeasurable, so there is no suffering of death. Having no parents, wives, or children, there is no suffering of being separated from those one loves. Being gathered among the assembly of supreme virtuous ones, there is no suffering of encountering those one hates.

With fragrant food served upon jeweled trays, one enjoys boundless resources; thus, there is no suffering of failing to obtain what one seeks, nor any suffering of exhaustion. Contemplating emptiness and stillness, there is no suffering of the aggregates (*skandha*). Out of compassion for sentient beings, one may manifest birth at will, yet does not abide in mere quiescence—this is the non-duality [of nirvana and samsara].

It is a vehicle. When wisdom illuminates birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one does not regress; such a person is no longer an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). If one is born in that land, there will be no afflictions. Those who do not hear or know this are truly to be pitied. Furthermore, there are virtuous persons who give rise to three kinds of lack of faith.

Those who do not seek rebirth there are all the more to be lamented. First, some say: "I shall transcend the Buddhas and the Patriarchs; Pure Land is not a place where I should be born. Second, some say: "Everywhere is pure land; there is no need to be born in the West. Third, some say:

"The holy realm of Ultimate Bliss is a place where we ordinary beings cannot be born. Now, the ocean of practice is inexhaustible. Although the *Lengqie Jing* contains a prophetic text stating that Nāgārjuna would see the Buddha-land of Amitābha as empty, Vimalakīrti constantly cultivated the pure land.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions offer praise with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the heart of going together. Try to reflect for yourself: who among us compares to these sages? To claim that one need not be born there—is this not self-deception? As for the patriarch Nāgārjuna, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a text that records his prediction in advance.

Maitreya is the master of the teachings; the *Treatise on Immeasurability* contains verses on seeking rebirth. They were all men of supreme wisdom who strove with diligence for rebirth in the Pure Land. To say that rebirth is unnecessary is nothing but self-contempt. A fire chariot may be extinguished, and a boat named "Non-Sinking" does not drown.

Those who manifest the fruits of their practice are more numerous than the sands of the Ganges. To transcend to the Supreme Place through ten recitations is no less swift than the case of Xiongjun, who entered hell but was revived to realize the wondrous cause.

The transgressions of worldly people are not necessarily like this; to claim one cannot be reborn is nothing but self-abandonment. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* records that the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla questioned Śākyamuni Buddha: "How can future sentient beings come to see the Buddhas of the ten directions? The Buddha instructed him to recite the name of Amitābha.

The Buddha then beheld all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Furthermore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If sentient beings from other regions hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, and are even able to give rise to a single thought of pure faith, joyfully loving and delighting in it."

All those who dedicate their roots of goodness and vow to be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life will, according to their vows, all be born there and attain non-retrogression; these are the words of the Buddha. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be trusted?

If one is not born in the Pure Land, what land could one be born in? To deceive oneself, to delude oneself, and to abandon one’s own spiritual nature, thereby flowing into the cycle of saṃsāra—whose fault is this?

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, with one mind and sincerity, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

In the preface to the *Longshu Jingtu Wen* (The Text on the Pure Land of Longshu), it is said: "The Tathāgata Amitābha, through the power of his great vows, gathers in all classes of beings. The invocation of his name is exceedingly simple, yet the realization of the fruit is exceedingly swift. Some have harbored doubts regarding this. I [Zhang]—*Note: The text here indicates the author's own reflection following the citation.*

I have once spoken of this for you: Amitābha Buddha is your very nature; the Land of Ultimate Bliss is your very mind. Sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, sinking into the seven realms of existence.

They establish a self and a Buddha, as if heaven and earth were separated by a vast chasm. For this reason, the Buddha, through his compassionate skillful means, reveals, awakens, and leads them into understanding. He manifests the various immeasurable *nirmita-samādhis* (transformed samādhis) to adorn that land, making it exquisitely magnificent and beautiful. Later, he employs his eloquent wisdom to expound upon it, causing all sentient beings to feel joy and delight.

If, amidst the activities of daily life, one can give rise to a single thought—recalling that Tathāgata and desiring to be born in that land—then this single thought, pure and firm, is nothing other than what belongs to one's own nature; it is no different from the Buddha. At that moment of mindfulness, do not give rise to...

While seated, Amitābha Buddha and the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) all appeared before him. He practiced in this manner until it reached full maturity. When his illusory body perished, this nature did not perish. A golden lotus pedestal arose from the seeds of his nature, and he was reborn therein as if returning to his own cottage.

All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were his kinsmen, for their nature is no different from his; thus, they naturally felt mutual affection. His friend Wang Xuzhong of Longshu was upright, serene, simple, and pure. He was widely learned in the various classics and had transmitted commentaries on the Six Classics and the various philosophical schools totaling hundreds of thousands of words.

One day, he pointed to them and said: "All of these are merely habitual karma; they are not the ultimate Dharma. I shall seek only my return to the West. From then on, he applied himself with diligence, contemplating only the Buddha. When he was nearly sixty years old, he spread...

Wearing coarse clothing and eating simple vegetables, he traveled a thousand *li* with calluses thick upon his feet. He taught others in this manner, never finding leisure to heed wind, rain, cold, or heat. When dwelling in seclusion, he called his practice "instruction" (*ke*), performing a thousand prostrations until the division of night before retiring; his face was radiant and luminous. Those who beheld him remarked that it was as if the text of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* were manifest.

Regarding all the methods of cultivation and the chapters on spiritual responses and realizations, they are recorded here in full from beginning to end. For those seeking to believe in the Way, I have had them carved into wood for circulation. Since you have entrusted me to write a preface for this book, I have thus inscribed these words at its head.
[Written by] Xu Zhong, named Ri-xiu, on the first day of the tenth month, at Li-yang. Zhang Xiao-xiang provides the preface.
Lungshu Xuzhong’s *Pure Land Dharma Gate Innkeeper’s Raincoat*:
An Exhortation to Prepare for Rebirth.

(Lungshu Jingtuwen states briefly: "For example, when entering a great city, one must first seek a place to settle before going out to attend to business. By evening, when it grows dark, there will be a place to lodge. 'Seeking a place to settle first' refers to practicing cultivation.")

This refers to the Pure Land. "Arriving at dusk when it grows dark" refers to the arrival of one's great destiny (the end of life). "Having a place to lodge" refers to being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms.

Furthermore, it is like preparing for rain before traveling far during the spring months. If a sudden downpour occurs, one will not suffer the distress of getting soaked or becoming disheveled. "Preparing for rain beforehand" refers to practicing the cultivation of the Pure Land. "A sudden downpour occurring" refers to the imminent exhaustion of one's life-force.

"Not suffering the distress of getting soaked or becoming disheveled" refers to not reaching the depths of the evil realms to undergo various afflictions. Moreover, "seeking a secure lodging beforehand" does not hinder the completion of one's business; "preparing for rain beforehand" does not hinder one's journey.

This is a long journey. For those who cultivate the Pure Land, there is no hindrance whatsoever to their engagement in all worldly affairs; why, then, would one not practice it? I have an acquaintance who, throughout his life, committed many sins of killing fish. In his later years, he fell ill with symptoms resembling a stroke.

I took pity on his transgressions and his suffering, so I went to see him and exhorted him to recite the name of Amitābha. He resolutely refused to recite it, speaking only of miscellaneous matters with me. Was this not because he was obstructed by his evil karma and clouded by his illness, such that he could no longer turn back?

Reflect thus: Once the eyes are closed for good, what can be done? Therefore, those who practice this path should urgently and swiftly turn their heads [toward the Way]. It is common knowledge to all people that day must inevitably be followed by night and cold by heat; these things cannot be concealed.

Yet, when it comes to the fact that birth must inevitably be followed by death, people avoid it and refuse to speak of it. How great is this delusion! This is because they do not realize that what is called the "self" never actually dies; rather, it merely passes away when the conditions of karma are exhausted.

For this reason, one must cultivate the Pure Land to seek rebirth within a lotus flower, thereby receiving a body of pure emptiness and infinite longevity to escape all the suffering and affliction of birth and death.
The Buddha showed this to Ānanda and exhorted ordinary beings to seek rebirth there. (Longshu said:

In the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*, one day Śākyamuni Buddha’s countenance was more extraordinary than usual. His attendant Ānanda, finding it strange, questioned him. The Buddha said: "Excellent is your question!

It surpasses the merit of making offerings to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, as well as bestowing gifts upon the devas, humans, and even down to the smallest crawling and flying insects, for as many as ten million kalpas; it would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of it. Why is this? Because the heavenly kings and emperors..."

"From the common people down to the smallest crawling insects, all shall attain the path of liberation through what you have asked. Observing this, it is evident that when Śākyamuni Buddha first intended to speak of Amitābha Buddha, his heart was moved and his countenance changed from its usual state;
thus, the manner in which Amitābha Buddha moves the various Buddhas is surely extraordinary, let alone how he moves all sentient beings.

When Ānanda questioned him and he replied, he declared that for the devas, kings, and people, down to the smallest crawling insects, all shall attain the path of liberation through what you have asked. This means that from the highest heavens down to the wriggling creatures,"

Since they are all within the three realms, they do not escape saṃsāra; therefore, they have not yet attained liberation. Yet, because the great power of Amitābha’s vows reaches everywhere, he delivers them all.

Consider his initial verse of aspiration: "When I attain Buddhahood, my fame shall transcend the ten directions. Humans and devas who joyfully hear it shall all come to be born in my land. Even those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm shall likewise be born within my land.

Thus, there is no one within the three realms or the cycle of the six paths of rebirth whom he does not deliver. For this reason, this sutra says: "Amitābha Buddha currently resides in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he teaches and transforms countless devas and humans."

Among the people down to the countless species of creeping and wriggling creatures, there are none who do not attain transcendence and liberation. "Creeping" refers to minute flying insects; "wriggling" refers to minute crawling worms. Even such beings as these, the Buddha still transforms and delivers.

How much more so for human beings! This is why his vast deliverance of sentient beings is without end; that a person might, in a single thought, take refuge [in him] and thereby be born in his land—of this there is no cause for doubt.
Benefiting both the present and the future, it encourages the laity to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].

While the discourse on the Pure Land is frequently encountered in daily life, its remaining merit is often perceived as occurring only after death. Those who do not understand stop there, regarding it merely as a matter for the afterlife; yet they fail to realize that it is of great benefit even during one's lifetime.

Why is this? Whatever the Buddha taught to instruct humanity was nothing but goodness. How does this differ from what the Confucian teachings use to instruct people? It is only that their names are different. Therefore, taking the Pure Land as one’s core concern—

Thus, that which manifests within the midst of daily life—what the mind contemplates, what the mouth speaks, and what the body performs—will, in every instance, be nothing but good. Being good, one becomes a gentleman or a great sage; in this present world, people will revere them and the deities will protect them; their fortune and rank may increase, and their lifespan may be extended.

Speaking from this perspective, who could say that following the Buddha’s words and taking the Pure Land as one's primary concern is of no benefit during one's lifetime? Next, there are those whose karmic conditions have deprived them of the ability to focus their will exclusively upon this path;

yet even for those who possess a mere fragment of such resolve, evil conditions will diminish from this point forward, and wholesome conditions can increase from this point forward. If one continues to diminish evil conditions without ceasing, they will ultimately reach the point of total eradication.

Their evils may persist, yet their wholesome conditions increase without ceasing; in the end, they will surely reach a state of pure goodness. Once evil is severed and goodness is purified, how could they not be considered gentlemen? How could they not be considered great sages?
Judging from this, who would say that those who follow the Buddha’s words and take the Pure Land as their primary concern receive no benefit during their lifetimes?

Furthermore, for those of the next lower grade—who do not know where propriety and righteousness lie, do not fear the terrors of punishment, and esteem only physical strength while pursuing only power and profit—if they come to know that they should take the Pure Land as their primary concern, they will surely come to know how to examine themselves and reproach their own faults. As it is said: "Though one cannot conform entirely to propriety and righteousness, one will at least draw near to them."

Although one may not be able to completely transcend the realm of punishment, one will certainly remain far removed from it. Gradually, one can escape the domain of the petty person (*puruṣa*) and ultimately find refuge as a noble person (*satpuruṣa*). That common people call themselves knowers of Buddhist principles and that the world regards them as virtuous individuals—this is the efficacy [of such practice].

From this perspective, who would say that following the words of the Buddha and taking the Pure Land as one's core concern is of no benefit to one's life? Someone might say: "If one follows the words of Confucius and takes Confucianism as one's core concern, would that not also be beneficial to one's life?

Why must it be the Pure Land? I reply: This is merely a worldly dharma (*laukika-dharma*); it is not a supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). Worldly dharmas do not transcend saṃsāra; supramundane dharmas...
Thus, one is directly liberated from the cycle of saṃsāra. That the Pure Land benefits both during one's lifetime and after death is because it encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
The cause is small while the fruit is vast; thus, I urge the multitude to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].

(There are nine grades of the Dharma-gate for practice; it can be cultivated by everyone. Even those who are sinful, the Buddha does not abandon. If one turns the mind toward the good, one becomes good.

Therefore, this Dharma-gate of ten recitations can be universally practiced by all. It is like a long-darkened room: a single lamp illuminates it, and it becomes bright. Thus, even those who have slaughtered oxen or horses—provided they lay down their butcher’s knife—can practice without difficulty. Nor does it hinder any worldly affairs.)

Therefore, whether one is in office, it does not hinder one's duties; as a scholar, it does not hinder study; as a merchant, it does not hinder trade; as a farmer, it does not hinder cultivation; in government service, it does not hinder administrative work;

and as a monk, it does not hinder meditation and recitation. In all such activities, nothing is mutually obstructed. Thus it is said: "The power of one's cultivation is seen in the brief interval of a single morning cup of tea. Consequently, this can serve as the indestructible capital for ten million kalpas. Why, then, would one not practice it?

Nowadays, there is a merchant who, by gaining two cents of profit on one cent, feels great joy, considering the interest earned to be substantial. Or a traveler who covers a journey that would normally take two days in a single day—[also feels great satisfaction].

One will surely rejoice, thinking that one has reached the required measure in abundance; this is because one knows joy when there is some small gain regarding external things. Or, if one receives the price of one coin for two coins, one will surely worry, thinking it is a loss of capital;

if one reaches the progress of one day in two days, one will also surely worry, thinking it is a waste of time. This is because one knows worry when there is some small loss regarding external things. Why then, regarding the limited light and time of our own bodies, do we pass it by in tears—our loss being so great—and yet not feel worry?

Regarding the fact that the conditions for the Pure Land are difficult to encounter, we have fortunately come to know them; this gain is so great, yet we do not feel joy. This is merely to see small gains and small losses [and react accordingly].

One may know their joys and sorrows, yet one cannot know the great matters of gain and loss; how can this be considered anything but extreme ignorance? Moreover, it requires no expenditure of time and involves very little effort, while the benefits received are truly beyond description.
Why, then, do you not cultivate it? Not to cultivate it—how lamentable! How lamentable!
Comparing merits and demerits to encourage the deluded to seek birth [in the Pure Land]:

It is not surprising that many do not believe when they first hear of the scenery of the Pure Land. This is because they are bound by what they see before their eyes; they assume that what is not seen before their eyes must likewise be nothing more than that.

For instance, one who dwells in a humble alley amidst filth and refuse—how could they know of a vast mansion’s purity? One whose vessel is small and whose food is of wild herbs—how could they know of the offerings presented before a meal? One whose storage is a tattered chest containing but a grain or two—how could they know of Heaven?

Because this world is so overflowing with abundance, those dwelling in the turbid world of *Sahā* do not believe that there exists a pure Buddha-land; thus they are born from a womb, unaware that there is birth by transformation within lotus flowers. Their lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, yet they are unaware that there is a lifespan as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

Clothing and food must necessarily result from labor, yet they are unaware that there is clothing and food provided spontaneously. Happiness is always intermingled with sorrow and affliction, yet they are unaware that there is singular, unadulterated happiness.

Therefore, one cannot fail to believe what the Buddha has spoken simply because it is not seen before one's eyes. Moreover, the Buddha strictly admonished that since a person should not speak falsely, he certainly would not deceive others with lies. As for those in the world who speak falsely, it is not [for the sake of... the Buddha.

One who seeks profit avoids harm. The Buddha has no desires for the world; how could he seek profit? The Buddha views birth and death as a sword cutting through empty space; how could he avoid harm? Thus, the Buddha has no occasion to employ false speech.

Among those in the world, even those of middling or superior character are unwilling to speak falsely, for it ruins their conduct—how much more so for the Buddha? His words are trustworthy and beyond doubt.
Clarifying the Ten Precepts: Exhorting Confucians to Seek Rebirth.

(Confucians may disparage the teachings of the Śākya clan because its followers lack preceptual conduct, and thus they do not believe in the Pure Land. This is not so. How can one disparage Laozi because some practitioners are unworthy, or disparage Confucius because some scholars are unworthy?

The wise do not reject words because of the person; how much less can one disparage the teachings because of their followers? The teachings of the Śākya clan contain both mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas. As for its mundane dharmas...)

The points upon which we Confucians agree cannot be enumerated in detail; let me briefly state the most significant ones. As for the Buddha’s methods of examining and instructing the world, they consist entirely of admonishing evil and encouraging goodness—and have we Confucians ever failed to do the same?

To take current examples: the Buddha regards killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the three karmas of the body, while Confucius spoke of "overcoming depravity and abolishing killing," and the Poets declared that "King Wen’s virtue reached even to the birds, beasts, and insects."

Is this not a warning against killing? As for theft, it is certainly not what is being discussed here. Confucius said, "I have not yet seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. The poets of the *Shi Jing* satirized those who do not love virtue but take pleasure in beautiful forms. Is this not a warning against sexual misconduct?

The Buddha regards false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech as the four karmas of the mouth. Confucius said, "If a person lacks trustworthiness, I know not how they can exist. Is this not a warning against false speech? He said, "Those with clever words and a pleasing countenance are far from possessing benevolence (*ren*).

Is this not a warning against frivolous talk? The *Book of Documents* says, "Do not follow me in my presence, only to speak otherwise behind my back. Is this not a warning against double-tongued speech? Harsh speech refers to the sounds of malice and anger that have not yet reached the level of foul language. Xunzi said:

Wounding words are more piercing than spears or halberds; whenever I see them, I never fail to warn against the mouths of malice and anger. Furthermore, the Buddha identifies greed, anger, and delusion as the three karmas of the mind. Confucius said, "Upon gaining something, one must consider its righteousness"; this is precisely a warning against greed.

It is said that Boyi and Shuqi did not dwell on past grievances; this is an admonition against anger. It is said that those who are in distress yet do not study are the lowest of the people; this is an admonition against ignorance. From this it may be seen that Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different.

The only point of difference is that the Confucians stop at worldly dharmas (*laukika-dharma*), whereas the Buddhists possess both worldly and supramundane (*lokottara*) dharmas. Because the Confucians stop at worldly dharmas, they speak only of a single lifetime and attribute [the outcome] to Heaven.

Because the Buddhists possess supramundane dharmas, they understand successive lifetimes and perceive the beginning and end of the karmic conditions of sentient beings. This is merely where they differ. If one wishes to know the strengths of Buddhism, one must examine the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Awakening of Faith*.

Regarding the *Bodhisattvapraśnottaratantra-sūtra* and the principles of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, if one has not yet attained such understanding and nonetheless proceeds to criticize them, then one must take heed of what Confucius said regarding those who "compose works without knowing [the truth].

If this is indeed the case, then the teachings of the Śākya clan are worthy of trust; how then can one fail to believe his words concerning the Pure Land? As for what is called the supramundane Dharma, the Pure Land is its most essential element; it is something that cannot but be diligently pursued.

One must diligently practice to sever [delusions] and exhort others to resolve to seek rebirth. (Regarding those in this world who are exclusively attached to their views, they say: "The Pure Land is but the pure mind; how could there be another Pure Land? Amitābha is one's own nature; there is no need to further behold Amitābha. This statement seems plausible but is not so. Why is this?

The Western Pure Land exists both in principle (*li*) and in manifestation (*ji*). If we discuss it in terms of principle, by being able to purify the mind, all things become pure; thus, it is truly the "Pure Land of the Mind Only" (*weixin jingtu*). If we discuss it in terms of manifestation, there actually exists the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). The Buddha has explained this with repeated and detailed earnestness.)

To speak thus—how could it be false? That every person can become a Buddha, and that what is called the "Self-nature Amitābha" is certainly not a falsehood. Yet, one ultimately has not yet reached this state. It is like fine timber that can be carved into objects and images of extreme beauty;

it must first undergo the labor of carving before it can achieve such perfection. It is impossible to point to the excellent material and immediately claim that the object or image is already beautiful.

To say that there is only the "Pure Land of Mind" and no further Pure Land, or that the "Self-nature Amitābha" makes it unnecessary to see Amitābha, is incorrect. Furthermore, some may believe in the existence of the Pure Land but, clinging to the doctrine of "Mind-only," claim that the Western Paradise is not worth being born in; all such views have missed the mark.

Why is this? These words are exceedingly lofty, and I fear they are not easily attained. An ancient said, "Only after seeing the Way does one cultivate it. It is also said, "A single wheel cannot move; a single wing cannot fly. Furthermore, the union of understanding and practice is called the Patriarchal Way.

Guifeng said, "The Buddha-nature is originally present, yet one must diligently cultivate; delusions are fundamentally non-existent, yet one must sever them. Our Master said, "If there is even a hair’s breadth of habitual leakage that is not exhausted, one will not escape wearing an iron collar and bearing a saddle, remaining to repay karmic debts elsewhere.

Now, my own mind can be the Pure Land, yet I have ultimately failed to make it the Pure Land; my own nature can be Amitābha, yet I have ultimately failed to become Amitābha. How can I neglect the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it, or disregard Amitābha and refuse to desire to see him? Great!

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "In the ten directions, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who have been reborn in the land of Amitābha. If even those bodhisattvas desire to be reborn there, what kind of person am I that I would not wish to be born there? Would this not mean that I am superior to all those bodhisattvas?"

A lay follower composed a literary eulogy, which moved a certain immortal (ṛṣi) to ride upon the clouds and listen to the Dharma from mid-air. Later, after seven months, Huiyuan again saw Amitābha Buddha’s body filling the void, with a circular halo containing various transformation Buddhas, while Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta stood in attendance to his right.

He said to Huiyuan, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days hence, you shall be born in my land. There, he saw the monks Buddhabhadra, Huichi, and Tanshun standing by the Buddha's side. They stepped forward, bowed to Huiyuan, and said:

"The Dharma Master’s aspiration preceded mine. Why have you arrived so late? Having seen this from afar with clear discernment, he spoke thus to his disciples, saying: "When I first resided here, I was fortunate enough to behold the sacred countenance of the Buddha three times in the Pure Land.

Now I behold it once more; my rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. The following day, he fell ill and lay in bed. What is the reason for this difference? The answer is: On the ground of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), there are no Buddhas and no sentient beings; there is neither pleasure nor suffering, neither longevity nor premature death. Furthermore, how could there be purity or defilement? How, then, could one still take arising or non-arising as the object of the mind?

This principle supersedes the phenomenal reality. Nevertheless, as for those dwelling within this realm: are they sentient beings, or are they Buddhas? If it is the realm of a Buddha, then they are not sentient beings; how then could there be suffering or joy, long life or premature death, purity or defilement? Try reflecting upon this yourself.

If you have not yet transcended the state of a sentient being, how can you fail to believe the scriptural teachings, and instead fail to resolve your mind on Amitābha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land? If it is pure, it is not defiled; if it is joyful, there is no suffering; if it is long life, there is no premature death.

To give rise to thought within non-thought and to seek birth within the unborn is to subvert principle with phenomena. As explained in the sutra, it is set forth in successive order:
the vows regarding the treasury of Dharma and the adornment through the cultivation of causes.

(The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles. At that time, there was a king who, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, gave rise to [the aspiration for]..."

He set his mind upon the Supreme Way, renouncing his kingdom and abdication of kingship to become a śramaṇa, taking the name Dharmākara. Possessing lofty talent, wisdom, and courage, he surpassed all in the world. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have resolved upon the Unsurpassed Way;

my vow is to expound the Dharma and for us to practice it together, so that I may swiftly attain perfect enlightenment in this world and uproot the very source of the suffering of birth and death. Then, the World-Honored One, King of Sovereign Power, for him expounded upon two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields, describing the good and evil, the coarse and the sublime lands of devas and humans.
Having heard this, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara practiced for five kalpas before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and, in his presence, formulated forty-eight extraordinary and supreme great vows.
The Forty-Eight Vows: The Vow Adorned by the Power of Vows that the Evil Realms Shall Have No Name (First:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be the names of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I never attain perfect enlightenment).
Second, the vow that none shall fall into the evil realms:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any sentient beings in my land who fall into the three evil realms, may I never attain perfect enlightenment."
The third vow for being of the same true golden color:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land are not all of the same true golden color, may I never attain perfect enlightenment."

Fourth: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land should have differences in physical appearance, such that some are handsome and others ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Fifth, the fulfillment of the vow regarding past lives:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land are unable to know their past lives and remain ignorant of events spanning hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
May I obtain the divine eye upon birth.

(Sixth: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land should not have the celestial limit [of vision] such that they cannot see hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)
Seventh: May I attain divine hearing upon birth.

(If, when I become a Buddha, the sentient beings in my land do not attain divine hearing and fail to hear the Dharma preached by hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)
Universal Knowledge of Mental Conduct and Vows (Eighth:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land lack the knowledge of others' minds and do not know the mental conduct of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The transcendence of supernormal powers through aspiration (Ninth:

If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the sentient beings of my land do not obtain supernormal powers such that they cannot, in a single thought-moment, traverse billions of Buddha-fields, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The vow for the perception of selflessness (the tenth:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should arise in the sentient beings of my land even a slight notion of 'I' and 'mine,' may I not attain perfect enlightenment").

The Vow of Certainty in Perfect Enlightenment (the eleventh: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the sentient beings of my land were not certain to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The Vow of Universal Radiance (Twelfth:

If, upon my attainment of Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land possess limited radiance that does not illuminate hundreds of thousands of billions of other Buddha-fields, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).

Thirteenth: Regarding the vow for infinite lifespan—“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land do not have an infinite lifespan, even for as many eons as can be calculated, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
[Fourteenth: Regarding] "Innumerable Śrāvakas.
(If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be no one able to know the number of śrāvakas in my land, and if there should be anyone who could know it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)
The fifteenth vow for the long life of sentient beings:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land do not possess an infinite lifespan (except for those who take birth through the power of their own vows), may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Sixteenth: "May all obtain a good reputation.
(If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are sentient beings in my land who possess an ill reputation, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)"
Seventeenth: May all Buddhas praise my vow.
(If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countless Buddhas within those immeasurable lands do not collectively praise my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)

The Vow of Rebirth through Ten Recitations (Eighteenth): If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of other lands hear my name and aspire to be born in my land, even if they recite it only ten times, yet fail to be reborn there— except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, who have slandered the true Dharma, or who have reviled the noble ones—
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
Nineteenth, the Vow to Appear Before Those at the Hour of Death:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in other lands who have resolved for Bodhicitta and wish to be born in Sukhāvatī should, at the time of their death, not see me appear before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Dedicating all roots of virtue with the aspiration:

(The twentieth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in other lands who hear my name dedicate their roots of virtue and aspire to be born in my land, yet this does not come to pass, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The Vow to be Endowed with Sublime Marks (the twenty-first: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land do not all possess the thirty-two marks, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).

Twenty-second: May all [the bodhisattvas] in my land attain the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), practicing the path of Samantabhadra; if this is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-third vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land do not present offerings to the countless Buddhas of other directions in the early morning and return to their own land before the mealtime—if this is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The fulfillment of all needs and wishes (the twenty-fourth:

If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there are Bodhisattvas in my land whose various requisites for making offerings and planting roots of goodness before the Buddhas are not fully perfected, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).

The twenty-fifth is the vow to skillfully enter fundamental wisdom: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land are not skillfully able to accord with and enter all-encompassing wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The twenty-sixth vow for the power of Nārāyaṇa:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land do not possess the firm and solid power of Nārāyaṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Adorning with Immeasurable Vows (The twenty-seventh:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there were anyone who could fully know or completely describe all the articles of adornment within my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).

Twenty-eighth: Regarding the wish for the jewel-trees to be fully known. (If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are immeasurable jewel-trees of various colors in my land that the assembly of bodhisattvas does not fully understand, I shall not take perfect enlightenment.)
Twenty-ninth, the vow for supreme eloquence:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land do not obtain supreme eloquence, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The Great Eloquence of Boundless Vows (the thirtieth:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land do not achieve boundless eloquence, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The Vow of the Pure Land’s Universal Radiance (The thirty-first:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is not pure and radiant, universally illuminating all Buddha-fields like the reflection of one's face appearing in a clear mirror, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The Thirty-second Vow for Immeasurable Supreme Sound:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should not be within my buddha-field immeasurable sounds that are extraordinary and surpass the world—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Vow Thirty-three: May all beings in the ten directions who are touched by my light attain peace and happiness. If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The Vow of Accomplishing Dhāraṇīs (the thirty-fourth:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, any Bodhisattvas in the ten directions who hear my name should not obtain dhāraṇīs, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
(Thirty-fifth: May I forever be free from the female body.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in any of the Buddha-lands who, upon hearing my name, attain pure faith and resolve their minds on Bodhi, yet do not come to be born again with a female body—then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)
The thirty-sixth vow: Hearing My Name and Reaching the Fruit.
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are bodhisattvas in all Buddha-lands who, having heard my name, do not practice until they reach Bodhi, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The thirty-seventh vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are Bodhisattvas in the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, give rise to a pure mind, yet are not honored and paid homage by all devas and humans, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

Thirty-eighth: Regarding clothing, may it be obtained according to one's thoughts and wishes. (If, when I attain Buddhahood, the clothing required by the sentient beings in my land should not arrive immediately upon being thought of, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)

The thirty-ninth: "If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, all classes of sentient beings who are born in my land do not immediately attain pure hearts and peaceful bliss like those of Arhats, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

The Vow for the Manifestation of Buddha-fields from Trees (Fortieth: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land who wish to see the pure lands of various Buddhas should not all be able to see them manifest within the jeweled trees—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
The Forty-first Vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings in other lands who, upon hearing my name, possess defective sense faculties or whose virtuous capacities are not extensive, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

The Vow for the Direct Realization of Samādhi (the forty-second: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, bodhisattvas in other realms should hear my name and yet fail to directly realize samādhi, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).

Forty-third: Upon hearing [my name], they shall be born into noble and wealthy families. (If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name do not, at the end of their lives, take birth into noble and wealthy families, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.)

The Forty-fourth Vow for the Fulfillment of Roots of Goodness: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name do not cultivate their roots of goodness, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Firm Vow to Make Offerings to Buddhas (The forty-fifth:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name should ever regress from making offerings to various buddhas until they reach enlightenment, may I not attain perfect awakening).

Forty-sixth: "I desire that they hear by themselves what they wish to hear. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who desire to hear the Dharma should not naturally be able to hear it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The Vow of Non-retrogression from Bodhi (Forty-seventh:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any bodhisattvas in other lands who, upon hearing my name, were to turn back from the mind of bodhi, may I not attain perfect enlightenment).
Forty-eighth: May I attain the stage of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi).

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name do not attain the stage of patience and do not manifest non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas, may I not take perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Bhikṣu Dharmākara of the past is now the Amitāyus Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. His land is magnificent and beautiful; his lifespan is immeasurable;
and his retinue is inconceivable—all of which have been accomplished through the great vows he made during his causal practice."
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this place of practice, as described in the sutras,

shall together with sincere resolve prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World, who is adorned by the causal practices of the Forty-eight Vows.

The Name of Amitābha: Adorned with Radiant Life.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra: "From here, to the west, passing through a hundred thousand billion buddha-fields, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma. Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called 'Utmost Bliss' (*Sukhāvatī*)?

Because the sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore called 'Utmost Bliss. Śāriputra, for what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?

That Buddha’s radiance is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction; for this reason he is named Amitābha. That Buddha’s lifespan, as well as that of his people, is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas; for this reason he is [named] Amitāyus."

Ānanda, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now. That Buddha has immeasurable śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats; they cannot be calculated by any means of reckoning.
You should know that the multitude of bodhisattvas is likewise so. In that Buddha-land, such meritorious adornments are perfected—this is his title.

The Contemplation of the Three Great Beings: The Adornment of the Precious Image (*Ārya-bhadrakalpika-sūtra*). The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to contemplate that Buddha should first visualize his image. Whether with eyes closed or open, they shall see a precious image with the color of Jāmbūnada gold, seated upon that flower. Once they have seen the image seated, their mental eye will open, and they will perceive everything clearly and distinctly.

They shall see the Land of Ultimate Bliss, adorned with the seven treasures, with its jeweled ground, jeweled ponds, and rows of jeweled trees. Celestial jeweled banners cover it from above, and nets of various jewels fill the void of space. Having seen these things, they must make them exceedingly clear."

[It is] clear, as if looking at the palm of one's hand. Having seen this matter, one should further visualize a great lotus flower to the left of the Buddha, exactly like the previous lotus, without any difference.

One should further visualize a great lotus flower to the right of the Buddha, and imagine the form of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara arising upon the seat of the left flower; he is also golden in color, no different from before. One should imagine the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta sitting upon the seat of the right flower.

When this visualization is accomplished, the images of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas all emit light. This light is golden in color and illuminates the various jewel trees. Beneath each tree there are also three lotus flowers, and upon each lotus flower is the image of one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, filling that land entirely. When this visualization is accomplished, the practitioner should...

One hears the sound of flowing water; the radiance and the various jewel-trees, as well as the wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, all preach the Dharma. Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly hears the wondrous Dharma. What the practitioner hears, upon emerging from concentration, is remembered and maintained without abandonment, and accords with the Sūtras.
If it does not accord, it is called a coarse perception (*audārikasaṃjñā*). To see the World of Ultimate Bliss is the perception of an image (*pratibimba-saṃjñā*).
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this place of practice, as previously described,

shall together with sincere resolve prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground before the name of Amitābha and his adorned precious image, taking refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the world.

The Land of Amitābha, adorned with ultimate bliss.
Today, the great assembly, with renewed sincerity, should listen attentively with a single mind. The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states:
Since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten minor kalpas have passed. The land where he resides is named Sukhāvatī, located precisely in the western direction.
It lies a distance of billions of Mount Sumerus from this Jambudvīpa realm. As for the ground of that land...
They were all composed of the seven natural treasures: first, the treasure of white silver; second, the treasure of gold; third, the treasure of crystal;
fourth, the treasure of lapis lazuli; fifth, the treasure of coral; sixth, the treasure of amber; and seventh, the treasure of musaragalva.
The ground is vast and expansive, exceedingly great and infinite. Each shines brilliantly, intermingling with light;
it is supremely soft, exquisite, and peerless among all the various jewels of the eight directions, above and below. These jewels are naturally conjoined and arise through transformation;
they are all the jewels of the sixth heaven. In that land, there are no seas, rivers, mountains, forests, or streams, whether large or small.
The valley has no place of darkness or obscurity; it knows neither spring, summer, autumn, nor winter, nor does it experience great cold or great heat.
It is always harmoniously temperate and exceedingly pleasant, beyond compare. There are all manner of natural things and foods of a hundred flavors.
Whatever one desires to obtain appears naturally before them. That which is not needed simply vanishes of its own accord.
Everything is according to their wishes. The land is entirely composed of bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women. Any woman who is reborn there immediately transforms into a man.
All have upright and handsome features, pure and exceptionally beautiful, and they are all of one uniform appearance, with none being deformed or ugly.
They are all courageous, sharp, and wise, wearing garments that appear spontaneously, and their minds dwell upon the Way and its Virtue.
Whenever they wish to speak, they all understand one another beforehand. Whatever they intend to say, they always speak of upright matters;
whatever they utter, they invariably speak of the Way of the Sūtras, never speaking other evil words. Their voices are like the sound of three hundred bells;
they all respect and love one another, harboring no jealousy or hatred, being like elder and younger brothers. All their minds are pure and clean, free from greed or longing. From themselves...
He knows from whence they came in previous lives and the time of their birth across billions of kalpas; he knows their past destinies, their virtues and evils, and their survival or demise.

He further knows that, according to the words of the Buddha of Infinite Light, among the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, all the devas, humans, and even the crawling and wriggling species who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha are reborn upon lotus flowers within ponds of the seven treasures.
They are born by spontaneous transformation (*upapāduka*) and grow naturally of their own accord; there is no one to nourish them with milk.
They all consume natural food and drink. Their bodies are neither the bodies of worldly humans nor the bodies of celestial beings.
They have all accumulated the virtue of manifold good deeds and have received bodies that are naturally empty and non-substantial, with forms of infinite extent.
Their exquisite beauty is beyond compare. The Buddha said: Regarding the dwellings of the seven treasures in which they reside, some are situated in the void of space and some are upon the earth.
If there is one who wishes for their dwelling to be the highest, the dwelling immediately becomes high; if there is one who wishes for it to be the greatest...
In the midst of empty space, all things are naturally according to one's will.

As for those among them who are utterly unable to cause their dwellings to conform to their wishes, it is because in previous lives, when seeking the Way, they lacked compassionate diligence. The Buddha said:

"All bodhisattvas and arhats possess the power of clear vision and penetrating hearing; they see and know the affairs of the eight directions, as well as the past, future, and present. Furthermore, they know that..."
The Buddha knows the thoughts and intentions—whether good or evil—of all beings in the heavens above and the world below, including even the smallest crawling insects;

he knows what they intend to say with their mouths, and he knows exactly in which year and in which kalpa each shall attain liberation, attain the human path, or be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.
He knows that they shall become bodhisattvas or arhats, knowing all these things through his conditions of wisdom. The Buddha said: "In the eight directions above..."
Countless gods, humans, and all classes of crawling and flying creatures from the lower realms who are born in the Land of Amitābha and are destined to become Buddhas are beyond measure;
those who have become arhats and attained the path of nirvāṇa are likewise countless and incalculable.
When Amitābha Buddha preaches the sutras for these bodhisattvas and arhats, [the assembly] is entirely...
A great assembly gathered; upon the lecture hall, there were bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, and human beings in incalculable numbers, beyond all reckoning.
They all flew to the place where the Buddha was, paid homage to him, and withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra.

The Buddha extensively expounded the Great Sutra of the Wisdom of the Path, and they all heard and understood it. There was none who did not rejoice and leap for joy; those whose minds were opened and liberated immediately—
Spontaneously, turbulent winds arose from the four directions and blew upon the trees made of the seven treasures, producing the sounds of the five musical notes.

The blossoms of the seven-treasure trees covered the entire land, all suspended in mid-air. The fragrance of these flowers descended throughout the kingdom and was scattered over the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
When the flowers fell to the ground, they formed a layer four inches thick; as soon as they began to wither slightly, the turbulent winds blew them away, clearing the withered petals.

They departed spontaneously. This occurred four times in succession. The Buddha said, "My second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the most peerless among the bodhisattvas and arhats of all buddha-fields.

In his flight and movement, his wisdom and valor, his clairvoyant vision and clairaudience, he knows the affairs of the eight directions—above, below, and across—and of the past, future, and present, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions."

Twofold. Combined together, they constitute a single wisdom. Even if one were to place such a person beside an Arhat in the land of Amitābha Buddha, their virtue would still fall short by hundreds of thousands of billions of times. The Buddha said:

"From the first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, to the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, up to the twenty-eighth heaven, all the devas and humans there possess ten thousand kinds of natural celestial [rewards]."
Objects of a hundred different colors, flowers, incense, silks and brocades, and *kārpāsa* and *kṣauma* garments;
ten thousand kinds of music, each more exquisite, beautiful, and superior than the last—each brought down from above to pay homage to and make offerings to Amitābha Buddha.
The Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and all the devas likewise performed great musical performances. At that time, the joy was beyond compare.
He said: "The various devas take turns opening the way for one another to avoid those who arrive later, and they continue to make offerings as before.

This continues until those who have become bodhisattvas all desire to become buddhas. Once they have become buddhas, they in turn teach and transform the devas, humans, and even the wriggling insects of the eight directions, above and below, desiring that they all likewise become buddhas. Once they have become buddhas," [the process repeats].
Furthermore, he instructs all the countless devas, humans, and species of crawling and flying creatures, causing them all to attain the path of Nirvana.
Those disciples who are capable of being instructed, in turn, instruct one another and successively deliver and liberate each other.

They have attained the four fruits of the path and the way of the Pratyekabuddha; they transform one another, delivering them across, so that all attain the way of Nirvāṇa in numbers beyond calculation.
Even when the kalpa ends, there will be no time of their final parinirvāṇa. The Buddha said:
"I have described the merits and the land of Amitābha Buddha as joyful and excellent for an entire night-long kalpa, yet it is still not finished. I have merely told you this brief account."
Listen! Today,
the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment— as described in the Great Sūtra— regarding the boundless adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the realm of Amitābha,
let us together with sincere resolve cast our bodies to the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

The precious river is pure, adorned with the waters of virtue.

The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are no mountains or seas, yet there are rivers. The waters of eightfold merit flow with deep currents, constantly surging and producing sublime, wondrous sounds, like the four thousand musical instruments of the devas;

the sound of these fills the world of Peace and Bliss. There are various famous flowers that drift downstream; when a gentle breeze stirs them, they emit all manner of fragrances. On both banks stand many sandalwood trees, their long branches and dense leaves interlacing to cover the river. They bear fruit and bloom with flowers, their fragrant radiance delightful to behold.

Beings roam there, coming and going as they please. Some may cross the river, bathing in the current and sporting in play; moved by the celestial waters, the water responds virtuously to all things, its depth, shallowness, coldness, and warmth perfectly accommodating the needs of each person."

Excellent, Ānanda. Beneath the great river, the ground is strewn with golden sand. There are various celestial fragrances, beyond all worldly comparison, which disperse their rich scent with the wind and mingle their perfume with the flowing waters.

When the people of that land go there for recreation, they are like those at the banks of a flowering river; though they possess the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), they ultimately cannot hear the sound of the surging currents. Yet, should any wish to hear it, they immediately attain realization through it—the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha in hundreds of thousands of varieties.

All sentient beings—whether already born, currently being born, or yet to be born—shall all obtain exquisite physical forms. Their features shall be upright and handsome, their spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) sovereign, and their merit complete. They shall enjoy various palaces, gardens, clothing, food, drink, incense, flowers, and necklaces, all according to their every need, entirely as they desire.
As they wish. Thus, having partaken of such food and drink, their physical strength and radiance increase, yet they have no excrement or urine.
The jeweled palaces are as they wish, with towers and pavilions magnificently adorned.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "If sentient beings require palaces, towers, or pavilions, according to their desires—whether high or low, long or short, broad or narrow, square or round—and with various couches and seats spread over with exquisite garments, all adorned with diverse kinds of jewels."
Before all sentient beings, it appears spontaneously; everyone thinks to themselves that they are each in their own palace.
Day and night are long and vast, and the divisions of time are magnificently adorned.

(The *Sūtra on Comparing the Merits of Buddha-fields* states: The Bodhisattva King of Inconceivable Radiance addressed the assembly, saying: "O sons of the Buddha, you should now listen attentively. If one were to measure the duration of time for this Sahā world throughout the full course of one great kalpa...")
This is one day and night in the land of Amitāyus Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment [should understand that], as described in the sutras, the precious rivers are pure and their days and nights are long and far-reaching.
With immeasurable adornment, with mutual sincerity and devotion, prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, we take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
