Twenty-four Joys: The Adornments of the Pure Land. (The *An-guo-chao* states: "That which is called 'Ultimate Bliss' possesses twenty-four joys: first, the joy of railings providing protection; second, the joy of jeweled nets covering the sky; third, the joy of tree-shades lining the thoroughfares; fourth, the joy of bathing pools made of the seven treasures;

fifth, the joy of the eight waters shimmering with ripples; sixth, the joy of seeing golden sand below; seventh, the joy of radiance at the edges of the steps; eighth, the joy of towers and terraces soaring into the void; ninth, the joy of the fragrance of the four types of lotuses; tenth, the joy of the ground being made of yellow gold; eleventh, the joy of the eight musical tones playing constantly... )

1. The joy of music; 2. The joy of the two flowers for twelve days and nights; 3. The joy of diligent exertion at dawn; 4. The joy of adorning and holding exquisite flowers; 5. The joy of making offerings to those in other directions; 6. The joy of walking meditation in one’s own land; 7. The joy of the harmonious singing of various birds; 8.

The joy of hearing the Dharma during the six periods of the day; 9. The joy of mindfulness of the Triple Gem; 10. The joy of being free from the three evil realms; 11. The joy of the Buddha’s emanations; 12. The joy of the trees shaking their jeweled nets.
Twenty-three: the joy of the twenty-three thousand lands sounding in unison. Twenty-four: the joy of the śrāvakas generating the bodhicitta.
Thirty types of benefit: the adornment of merit (*guṇa-vyūha*). The *Qun yilun* states:

"In the Western Pure Land there are thirty kinds of benefits: first, the benefit of enjoying the pure Buddha-land; second, the benefit of attaining the great Dharma-joy; third, the benefit of being in close proximity to the Buddha’s lifespan; fourth, the benefit of traveling through the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas."

1. The benefit of visiting the abodes of all Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and receiving predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). 2. The benefit of swiftly attaining the full perfection of the provisions of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*). 3. The benefit of quickly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

4. The benefit of gods and humans alike gathering together in a single assembly. 5. The benefit of never again falling back from the path. 6. The benefit of immeasurable practices and vows increasing and progressing in every moment of thought. 7. The benefit of the parrots and śāris proclaiming the sounds of the Dharma. 8. The benefit of the pure wind moving the trees like the sound of various musical instruments. 9.

The benefit of the mani-jewel vortices proclaiming suffering and emptiness (*duḥkha-śūnyatā*). 10. The benefit of all musical sounds playing forth myriad wondrous melodies. 11. The benefit of the forty-eight vows forever severing the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*). 12. The benefit of the true golden-colored body. 13. [The benefit of...]

18. The benefit of being fully endowed with the eighteen [attributes] and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). 19. The benefit of eternally abiding in the stage of certainty (*niyāma*). 20. The benefit of being free from all unwholesome states. 21. The benefit of a long and far-reaching lifespan. 22.

The benefit of food and clothing appearing spontaneously. 23. The benefit of experiencing only manifold joys. 24. The benefit of possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). 25. The benefit of having no actual women present. 26. The benefit of having no followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). 27.

The benefit of being free from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). 28. The benefit of attaining the three types of patience (*kṣānti*). 29. The benefit of the body possessing a constant radiance. 30. The benefit of attaining the body of Nārāyaṇa. The above is a brief description; the benefits of the Dharma are boundless. The realm of the Sages is not empty; this is a true discourse.
It is not erroneous. Today,
the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, with all the adornments as previously described,
shall together with sincere resolve cast their bodies to the ground in five-limbed prostration and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

This supreme and wondrous realm, with its pure lands throughout the ten directions and the palaces of the various heavenly kings, has no equal.

Therefore, we and all sentient beings vow to go to that land, together to enjoy all manner of adornments and inexhaustible happiness, to attain eternal purity, and to forever bid farewell to the four realms of rebirth.
May we behold Amitābha face-to-face and personally receive his prediction of enlightenment. [The six perfections and the four...]

Thus, there was nothing he did not fully practice. He possessed the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), attained the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha, and his body was adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
His supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) were unimpeded, and having entered the adamantine mind (*vajra-citta*), he realized equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Ritual for Repentance at the Amitābha Practice Hall, Scroll Six.
Part Six: Repenting of Karmic Obstructions.

Now, regarding the ritual of repentance for karmic obstructions: "Ritual" (*li*) refers to prostrating before the Buddha; "repentance" (*chan*) refers to confessing one's transgressions. The true nature (*bhūtatathatā*) is fundamentally empty and has never possessed a single thing. Once the deluded mind arises, however, there emerge ten thousand manifestations. This is the primary source from which transgressions originate. From this, the three poisons arise within, giving rise to the ten evil deeds;

they manifest outwardly such that every step taken is entirely ignorance (*avidyā*). Every object encountered becomes a link in the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and thus causes and conditions remain unbroken. Within the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), birth and death are inexhaustible. Even when born in the heavens, one constantly encounters the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*);

dwelling among humans, one perpetually suffers the eight hardships (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*). There is nothing that exceeds the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*), and it is difficult to escape the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). Abiding together in saṃsāra, one has not yet received liberation. If one wishes to achieve the fruit of purity, one must repent the causes of karma. Thus, faith and compassion must meet one another.

Then what sin would not be eliminated? When the ordinary and the sagely communicate, what hindrance would not be dispelled? Those who wish to enter the path of rebirth in the Pure Land must return to the gateway of prostration and repentance. Once karmic obstacles have been eliminated, body and mind will necessarily become pure.

The six sense-gates will grow still, and the long-accumulated dust shall vanish entirely. The single nature, perfectly luminous, will surely manifest its original radiance. It is simply that once the snow has melted away, spring will naturally arrive.
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice has already extensively elucidated the supreme and wondrous joys of the adornments of Sukhāvatī.

Having completed our shared rejoicing, we are filled with immeasurable joy and marvel at this unprecedented occasion. We shall now proceed to set forth a brief exposition in two sections for the purpose of confession:
first, the confession of one’s own self; second, the representation of one’s parents. Regarding the first, as the single mind is activated toward the Triple Gem—
Returning once more, each of you should cultivate sincere devotion, seeking compassion and confessing your transgressions:

"We, the sons of the Buddha, since beginningless and vast kalpas past, have had our minds shrouded by ignorance and been deluded regarding our own Buddha-wisdom. Through false confusion we have created karma, wandering through the cycle of birth and death.

We have turned our backs on the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, following evil teachers and friends. Our faculty of sight clings to forms, making us slaves to affection and craving; thus, we fail to behold the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body."
Pervasive throughout, the ear craves the realm of sound, resulting in endless harm; it fails to hear the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma of the perfect voice.
The nose craves fragrant odors, whereby the fetters arise; it cannot perceive the sublime fragrance of merit. The tongue craves various flavors, devouring sentient beings;

it indulges in false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued slander, reviling the Triple Gem and insulting one's elders and kin—how could such a tongue ever partake of [the true flavor]?
The Tathāgata’s profound flavor of the Dharma touches the faculty of the body; one becomes addicted to it without end, wandering in delusion day and night, never knowing contentment.
Thus, one commits all manner of evils, practicing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, such that the compassionate light of the Buddhas cannot illuminate or reach them.
When the faculty of the mind clings to dharmas, it grasps at objects and conditions, constantly giving rise to greed, anger, and false views in every thought-moment. All evils proceed from the mind.
Rooted in birth, how could one know the Tathāgata’s profound realm of reality? With the six sense faculties and three types of action, they have committed all manner of sins, revolving endlessly.
They have completely obstructed all wholesome virtues, being unable to give rise to the mind of great bodhi, nor able to practice any wholesome dharmas.
For a long night they undergo suffering without weariness. Such transgressions as these are known and perceived only by the Buddha; may he take them all into account.

Through this ritual repentance, may the continuity [of afflictions] be forever severed. Furthermore, these karmic obstacles arise from inversion; they possess no fixed reality and are fundamentally empty and quiescent.
I only pray that Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter will let the sun of wisdom shed its light to dissolve the frost and dew of the karmic delusions within my body and mind;
that the wind of compassion will universally blow to shatter the mountains of heavy karma; and that the long-flowing waters of Dharma will wash away the defilements of my heart. I only pray...

May we, together with our parents, swiftly reach the fundamental source of the mind and eternally extinguish the roots of transgression. May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm equally attain purity.
Furthermore, we take refuge in the Three Jewels and the immeasurable worthies and sages of the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space.
(One prostration). Today,
the great assembly, for the sake of severing the immeasurable knots of enmity and karmic obstacles within themselves, with singular, piercing sincerity,
cast their bodies to the ground in five-limbed prostration and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment, with renewed sincerity, seeks compassion and repents. All members of the assembly should reflect as follows:
In the past, while my parents were among men, they incurred the calamity of endangering their own lives due to the private affection for their child.

Because of the accumulated misfortunes resulting from this, the retribution has now reached my kin. Bowing my head and reflecting deeply upon this, my grief and anguish increase greatly. Now I extend my life to take refuge and, shedding tears of blood, I beg for mercy.
I pray that by relying on the majesty of the Triple Gem, the transgressions of my two parents may be extinguished, and that we may together prostrate ourselves with our five limbs in profound sorrow.
They prostrated themselves on the ground, choked with grief and sobbing, their tears flowing like rain.

We disciples [Name], on behalf of our parents, kinsmen, and relatives within the *dharmadhātu* from beginningless kalpas until this day, now before Amitābha and the Triple Gem of the ten directions, contemplate with a sincere heart:
my parents, due to ignorance and attachment in the past, cherished and protected my body as the Sūtra describes...
They spoke thus: "While harboring deep attachment and providing protection, they turned the damp to dry for us; they swallowed the bitter while spitting out the sweet.

They nurtured us with milk and sustenance until, in their ultimate compassion, we committed boundless sins—deceiving the worthy and slandering the sages. While they provided us with clothing and food, we slaughtered living beings to nourish our own mouths and bellies.
Deluded and inverted by ignorance, we were entangled in foolish craving until our lives ended and we sank into the evil realms—all because of them."
Due to the karmic burdens of my past lives, I now take the place of my parents in this body.

From the beginning until now, there is no evil among the ten paths of unwholesome action—such as killing, stealing, impure sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh words, double-tongued speech, greed, anger, and ignorance—that has not been fiercely committed by me.
Following false teachers, I lacked faith in the Triple Gem, or I violated the five [precepts].

Whether observing the eight precepts, the ten precepts, or even the full set of monastic vows, there are those who are icchantikas who deny cause and effect, slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, and destroy the wholesome deeds of others.
Lacking a heart of compassion, they refuse to joyfully encourage their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life;
they go so far as to kill their fathers and mothers, kill their upādhyāyas and ācāryas, shed the blood of a Buddha, and disrupt the *karmavācanā* and the turning of the Dharma wheel.

They have driven a wedge between the Saṃgha; they have killed Arhats; they have destroyed stupas and ruined monasteries; they have mutilated and destroyed scriptures and images; they have conscripted monks into labor or forced them to abandon the Path;

they have misappropriated the wealth and property of the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions in both the present and the future; they have preached the Dharma with impurity and defiled those who practice the Brahma-faring life.
Thus, they have committed various kinds of offenses against the Triple Gem, their teachers, their parents, and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.
Sins—whether committed by oneself, taught to others, witnessed being committed, or rejoiced in—occur in ever-increasing layers. These layers are inexhaustible;
they pervade the entire Dharma-realm and fill all of space. Now, before Amitābha Buddha, I repent them all.

By the majestic spiritual power of Amitābha Buddha, may they be dissolved like ice in hot water, and may I, in accordance with this thought, be transformed into unsurpassed wisdom and enlightenment. Furthermore, A...
The forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, emit pure light to gather them in and never abandon them.
His dwelling, Sukhāvatī, is adorned with myriad jewels; bodhisattvas who are reborn there shall never regress. They practice without interruption until they reach enlightenment.
Our Teacher Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the ten directions earnestly exhort and praise this single thought-moment.
Even with as few as ten recitations, from one day up to seven days, by calling the Name and maintaining focused mindfulness, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain.

Yet we, being ignorant and deluded, neither believe nor comply; sometimes, having heard this, our hearts respond with derisive laughter. Upon seeing those who practice nianfo, we harbor malicious intent and disparage them.
Even if there are those who do believe, they lack a resolute mind; their karmic conditions are deep and heavy, entangled in worldly affairs, and their bodies remain [bound].

At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), their minds dwell upon conventional truth while their mouths speak of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; yet their hearts remain attached to this Sahā world. When practicing the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), their minds are largely distracted and agitated.
Thus, not a single fragment of goodness is accomplished through the three types of pure karma, nor is even one matter mastered regarding the sixteen contemplations of the mind.

Though they have left the household life, they do not cultivate the conduct of the Saṃgha; they crave only gain and offerings, violate the precepts and break the fasts, and deceive sentient beings by falsely claiming—

Master, you have preached what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and preached the Dharma as what is not the Dharma. You claimed to have attained what you had not attained, and claimed to have realized what you had not realized.
Your mouth speaks of emptiness, yet your steps walk within existence. You are devoid of shame and lack of conscience; you are neither awakened nor aware.

Such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless; I pray that you will grant their extinction. Furthermore, there are sentient beings who do not believe that leaving the household life is the path to liberation, and who are deeply attached to...

Attached to the five desires, they take no pleasure in rebirth in the higher realms nor do they cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). They feign being virtuous people, holding prayer beads in their hands while harboring poison and evil in their hearts.
They indulge recklessly in ignorance and stubbornly engage in strife, arbitrarily giving rise to disputes and failing to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

They openly associate with evil friends to disturb and confuse practitioners. Sinking themselves and sinking others, they become the seed of hell. Possessing demons here and there, they obstruct the pure path.
Born of the earth, such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless; I pray that they may be extinguished.

At the time of death, one may encounter an untimely demise—such as a wall collapsing, a house falling, a tree breaking, or a cliff crumbling; or being swept away by water or consumed by fire; or being harmed by insects or bitten by beasts;

or when weapons suddenly arrive, or poison causes sudden injury, or a terminal illness strikes the body, leaving no leisure to recite the Buddha’s name; or when one is entangled in a protracted, grave illness and suffers.
Their bodies and minds are oppressed; they writhe and cry out, unable to settle their right mindfulness.

Should they lack virtuous friends to assist them in developing pure causes, then due to these various karmic obstacles and conditions, at the time of death they shall not behold the Buddha nor attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Instead, they will wander through the five turbidities of this Sahā world, taking birth according to their karma within the three miserable realms and eight difficulties. Therein, they will suffer the five pains and five burnings to the utmost.

It is extreme suffering. There will be no end to future births and deaths. One may fall into the calamity of being born from a womb with golden shackles, unable to see a Buddha for five hundred years.
All of this arises from having, since the distant past, lacked faith in Amitābha Buddha and lacked faith in rebirth in the Pure Land;
due to the karma of body, speech, and mind involving contempt and slander, even though one has now resolved [to practice],...

My mind is beset by many obstacles and difficulties. I now prostrate before Amitābha Buddha; I pray that with your divine eye, divine ear, and knowledge of others' minds, and through your great kindness and compassion, you will take pity on me, accept me, and hear my confession.

May this cause my parents and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm to be freed from the obstacle of retribution, the obstacle of karma, the obstacle of afflictions, the obstacle of disbelief in the Buddha’s words, and the obstacle of having no joy in practice. Five...
May all obstacles of the turbid and evil age, the obstacles of the borderlands and the city of doubt, and the obstacles of not hearing of the Triple Gem— indeed,
every obstacle to rebirth even as small as a single hair— be entirely eliminated. May all become pure, with right faith manifesting before them, free from doubt and non-retrogression,
so that they may certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, swiftly attain perfect enlightenment, turn the Great Dharma Wheel, and fulfill the vast and great vows of Samantabhadra.
[Proceeding with] the practice. Having finished the repentance, take refuge and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha.

Today, for the sake of the great assembly of fellow practitioners in this *maṇḍala*, and furthermore universally for all immeasurable sentient beings of the four modes of birth and six realms, as well as for the parents of oneself and others—whether lay or ordained—who have, from beginningless time until now, committed various karmic offenses that create obstacles:
Regarding the path to rebirth in the Pure Land, I pray that all obstacles to birth there and all karmic hindrances be granted remission and extinguished.
With a single-minded and sincere resolve, equally and most earnestly prostrating with our five limbs touching the ground, we take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

They revolve through the six realms of existence, receiving bodies born from the four modes of birth—whether male, female, or neither male nor female—pervading all places and giving rise to immeasurable offenses.
Some become large-bodied beings who prey upon one another, while others become minute-bodied beings.

They prey upon one another, the strong bullying the weak. Through such karmic acts of mutual devouring and killing, they create immeasurable and boundless obstacles to the bodhicitta, obstacles to the bodhisattva vow, obstacles to the bodhisattva practice, and obstacles to rebirth in a pure land. Today, I repent.
I pray that you will grant their eradication. From beginningless time until this very day, [Name] and others have undergone the bodies of the four modes of birth within the six realms of existence.
During this interval, the evils we have committed are infinite and inexhaustible.

Such transgressions as these are known and seen in their entirety only by the Buddhas and Great Earth Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

Whatever has been known and seen, and however much of the evil karma has been committed, today we sincerely prostrate ourselves with our heads to the ground, seeking compassion. With shame and remorse, we repent:

Homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent Amitābha Buddha of the Western Pure Land, the World of Ultimate Bliss, who shares the same name and title with three hundred and sixty trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred Buddhas.

(The above is the name of the Buddha, known as Maitreya [Amitābha]. The *Precious King Treatise* states: During the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, there were an old man and an old woman who used one *dǒu* of grain to count their recitations as they called upon the name of Amitābha Buddha, vowing to be reborn in the West.)

The Buddha said, "I have another expedient means to enable you to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha such that one recitation yields the merit of many grains of rice. I shall therefore teach you to recite the names of the Buddhas above. Let us verify this with pure grain: six million grains of millet make one *dou*;

sixty million grains make one *shuo*; six hundred million make ten *shuo*; six billion make one hundred *shuo*; sixty billion grains make one thousand *shuo*; six hundred billion grains make ten thousand *shuo*; and six trillion grains make one hundred thousand *shuo*. The number of these Buddha-names is precisely six hundred thousand *shuo*.

This allows for one *he*, nine *shao*, and nine *chao*—the count of one hundred grains—to equal the merit of half an eon within a single recitation. By teaching these two elderly people according to this method, then..."
The merit is exceedingly great; it can extinguish the sins of immeasurable kalpas (from the *Jueyi ji*).

VII. Arousing the Bodhicitta Now, as for arousing the bodhicitta:

it is the doorway to the True, the foundation for the stages of the Sages. It is because of this that the Buddhas of antiquity attained completion, and by means of this that the Enlightened Ones of old realized their realization. It is the foremost of all practices and the source of all mental states; it stands at the very beginning of the five stages.

It serves as the pouch and bag for the three vehicles, sometimes receiving the veneration of Megha; for the initial mind is not different from the final mind. It may even be ranked before the Arhat, for a minor fruit cannot be equated with a great fruit—its inexhaustible merit is beyond measure.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice has together completed the rites of confession for both self and others; our karmic obstructions have been cleared, and our bodies and minds are pure.
We are now fit to resolve to awaken the great bodhicitta and may thus seek rebirth in the Pure Land; each of you should therefore cultivate a sincere and earnest resolve.
Filled with joy and exultation, they take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Regarding the second [category], the practice of superior cultivation, two types are briefly presented: either practicing one specific aspect exclusively, or practicing all eight dharmas together.

As for the first, the Sūtra states: "If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to that name for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, then at the time of their death, Amitābha..."
Amitābha Buddha will appear before one, and one shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This single practice fully encompasses three mentalities:

first, the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because one maintains right mindfulness of the *dharmatā* (the nature of reality) [realizing that in every thought, the Dharma-nature body is the very mind and the Buddha, for it is the true Dharma-body];

second, the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because one delights in cultivating all virtuous practices [restraining body and speech, benefiting oneself and others, practicing the six perfections, universally upholding the Three Refuges, and clearly maintaining these in mind].

These are collectively termed "mindfulness" (念). Third is the mind of great compassion, because it rescues all sentient beings from suffering (this explains the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, as it delivers all sentient beings from the three sufferings and the eight sufferings).
First, one must possess these three minds while practicing diligence; second, regarding the practitioner who possesses the eight dharmas, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"One who accomplishes the practice of the eight dharmas will be free from blemish and be reborn in the Pure Land. These are: benefiting sentient beings without expecting a reward; [and so forth].
On behalf of all sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions, he dedicates all the merit he has created entirely to them.

He regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind, remaining humble and unobstructed. Toward all bodhisattvas, he views them as if they were Buddhas. When he hears sutras he has not heard before, he does not doubt them.
He does not conflict with the śrāvakas; he does not envy the offerings given to others, nor does he exalt his own benefits. And regarding them...
Within this, one should subdue the mind, constantly examine one's own faults, and not speak of the shortcomings of others; always with a single mind, one should seek all merits.

These eight causes comprehensively encompass the five vows. Having recognized that the practice for rebirth is inseparable from the five vows and three minds, each person should reverently accord with them. As the verse says:
I look up and address all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless realms of the ten directions:
from this day forth, I shall seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and vow to give rise to the bodhicitta.
I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings; I vow to accumulate boundless merit and wisdom.
I vow to study the boundless Buddha-dharma; I vow to serve the Tathāgatas without end;
I vow to realize unsurpassed Bodhi.

Furthermore, as for those who practice by way of abandoning marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they rely on words and become attached to marks, thereby increasing the fetters of birth and death. They abandon phenomena and return to...
Truly so. One realizes the eternal bliss of Nirvana; how much more so when one desires the spirit to dwell in the Pure Land! It is essential that the mind realize the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If one can perceive the spiritual source upon every encounter with the eyes, then these very worldly conditions become a pure land (*viśuddhakṣetra*). As the verse says:
The awakened mind now realized is free from all intrinsic natures and characteristics;
it is devoid of the grasping at the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so forth, as well as the duality of grasper and grasped.
All phenomena are entirely selfless, equal to space, and one’s own mind is fundamentally unarisen. Because emptiness is perfectly quiescent, it is like that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
I too have thus aroused the great bodhicitta; therefore, with a sincere heart, I pay homage today to the great assembly.
Regarding the supreme practice of rebirth, mindfulness of the Buddha comes first. It is perfected through the fulfillment of the eight causes and the cultivation of the five vows.

To fully realize that the pure land is mind-only, one must rely upon bodhi free from signs. With a sincere mind and all five limbs prostrate on the ground, take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

*The Armor of Repentance for the Ritual of Contemplation and Recitation at the Altar of Amitābha*, Scroll Seven:
Chapter Eight, On Vowing to Be Reborn in the Pure Land.

Now, those who aspire to be born in the Pure Land follow the words of Śākyamuni’s special praise and respond to the vow of Dharmākara to deliver sentient beings. At the moment of death, they will be moved by the arrival of the holy assembly to welcome them; at the time of birth, they will receive the guidance of Amitābha.

Entrusting our substance within the pool of the seven treasures, we shall be born by transformation amidst the nine grades of lotuses. Our lifespan shall be unfathomable and our bodily radiance immeasurable; we shall attain the wisdom of the seven eloquences and possess the majesty of the six supernormal powers. With Bodhisattvas as neighbors and Śrāvakas as companions—just as it is for us, so it shall be for all sentient beings.

Even those as stubborn as iron or stone shall have their hearts turn toward the Golden World (Suvarṇabhāsottama-kṣetra). May this King of Vows alone not forsake them, but guide them at every moment into the lotus pond.
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice has together brought forth the great bodhicitta.

We should know that from this day forward, we are born into the family of the Tathāgata, become sons of the Dharma King, join the ranks of the pure assembly, and succeed those who have attained rebirth there.
Therefore, we must further cultivate and train in the practices and vows of bodhi, just as Amitābha Buddha did during his initial causal stage.

I shall likewise practice and study in succession the forty-eight vows made by the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, as well as the vast practices and vows of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, and all the practices and vows of the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
May we be born together in the Pure Land. With the five limbs prostrate on the ground, I take refuge in the Great One of the World.
Compassionate Father.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice makes this vow with a sincere heart: may [the name of the person] and others universally extend [this merit] to the four debts of gratitude and the three...
There are sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who, from this day forward, shall abide in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), cultivate the true causes for the pure karma of the Buddhas,

provide filial support to their parents, serve their teachers and elders, maintain a compassionate heart and refrain from killing, practice the ten wholesome actions, receive and uphold the Three Refuges,
be fully endowed with the various precepts, not violate the rules of dignified conduct, resolve upon Bodhicitta, have deep faith in cause and effect, and recite the Great [Vehicle]...
This vehicle encourages practitioners to be mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, giving,
and the heavens; with a sincere mind, a profound mind, and a mind of dedication and aspiration, they invoke the names of the Buddhas, praise their radiant light,

contemplate the sixteen wondrous realms of the Buddha’s primary and secondary environments, recollect the forty-eight original vows of the Buddha, weigh the three grades of rebirth, and enter deeply into the five gates.
Following the three gates of Bodhi, we faithfully accept the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Whether with a distracted mind or a concentrated mind, we cultivate mundane and supramundane virtues. Relying on the sutras to give rise to practice, we take the end of our lives as our limit.

We pray that the holy power of Amitābha Buddha will secretly bestow its grace and his supernormal powers will manifest their benefits, enabling us to concentrate our spirits upon the path of awakening and tread securely upon the Great Way in every movement.
In their majestic deportment, they never cease beholding the Buddha, as if holding a bright mirror and seeing the reflection of one's own face.

Furthermore, within dreams, they constantly see the various wondrous and joyful events of that land, which gladden and delight my heart, causing my progress to increase. Through his compassionate protection, the seeds of the Dharma flourish;

sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they remain far removed from demonic activities. Moreover, the karmic afflictions and worldly toil accumulated over immeasurable kalpas [are likewise purified].

All these constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Through the roots of goodness and merit, they enter together into the great cause; having accumulated all conditions, they are collectively dedicated [to enlightenment].

At the time of death, there shall be no obstacles or difficulties. Seven days prior to the end of life, one will know in advance that the time has arrived, and the body will be free from pain and suffering.
The mind is free from delusion, and body and mind are peaceful and blissful, as if entering meditative concentration.

Upon encountering a virtuous friend who instructs them to perform the ten recitations, Amitābha Buddha and his assembly of holy beings appear before them, emitting great radiance and extending their hands to welcome them.
One sees oneself mounted upon a vajra pedestal, following behind the Buddha; in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, one is reborn in that land.
Having been reborn in that land, one beholds the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all the marks of excellence, and beholds the bodhisattvas, complete with all their marks of excellence.
In the Forest of Radiant Jewels, they expound the sublime Dharma; having heard it, they immediately realize the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Their bodies become the color of pure gold, equal and without distinction, endowed with the thirty-two marks and mastery of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), possessing great eloquence, and expounding all-encompassing wisdom.
With bodies like those of Nārāyaṇa, their lifespans are immeasurable; they receive offerings according to their wishes, and exquisite robes appear spontaneously.
They never hear ill repute and are not attached to the view of a self. All these supreme and virtuous people assemble in one place, dwelling in the stage of right determination, never falling back.

Ultimately reaching the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they enjoy the pure Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss. Six times throughout the day and night, they make offerings to Amitābha Buddha;
every morning at dawn, they serve the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, hearing the Dharma and receiving predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Having attained the dhāraṇīs, they exercise mastery over emanated bodies, pervading the ten directions. In lands where no Buddha resides, they manifest perfect enlightenment;

in places of extreme suffering, they sport with supernormal powers. According to the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the scope of what is to be known, they manifest physical bodies before them.
Day and night they preached the Dharma without ceasing. In every thought-moment, they caused unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta;
in every thought-moment, they caused unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
May the provisions of merit and wisdom be fully perfected, so that we may together attain unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment and each adorn a pure land and gather and transform sentient beings, exactly like Amitābha Buddha, without any difference.
We pray that Amitābha Buddha will compassionately bear witness to this.
Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment makes this vow: May all sentient beings fully possess the pure Buddha-lands of Bodhisattvas;
may they joyfully transform stinginess and jealousy and completely deliver others from all evils; may they gather in those in the eight difficult states and those who harbor contention and anger.
Diligently practicing all manner of goodness, they gather in those who are indolent; through meditative concentration and supernormal powers, they gather in those with distracted thoughts.

Having completed their vows, they together, with sincere hearts, prostrate themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching the earth, taking refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment shall each individually make such a vow, tracing back to the origin of all evils. All...

It takes the six sense faculties as its object. These six faculties are the root of all calamities; yet, although they are the root of calamity, they can also cultivate and accumulate immeasurable meritorious deeds.
Thus, the Śrīmālā-sūtra says: "Guard the six faculties and purify body, speech, and mind.
Using this principle as proof that they are the basis for generating goodness, one should give rise to great vows regarding these six faculties.

I first give rise to this vow for the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment today, and extend it widely to all sentient beings of the four modes of birth and six realms throughout the ten directions:
from this moment until the time of our final rebirth, may our eyes never again behold any of the worlds of *saṃsāra*.

May all evil and unwholesome forms cease; may my eyes always behold the Western Amitābha Buddha’s Jāmbūnada-golden body with its eighty-four thousand marks and signs that accord with his form, the purple-gold bodies of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude, their upright and subtle beauty, the thirty-two marks, and the infinite adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

With a pure countenance, they constantly see all sentient beings being reborn in the Pure Land, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and receiving the prophecy of enlightenment before their very eyes;

with a joyful countenance, having completed their vows regarding the faculty of sight, they together, with sincere resolve, prostrate themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching the earth and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

"Furthermore, I vow that today, may the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, and by extension all beings of the four modes of birth and six realms throughout the ten directions..."
Sentient beings, from this day forth until their rebirth, may they always know that greed, anger, and ignorance are afflictions in this Sahā world;
may they always know that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech are afflictions;
and may they always know the offenses of killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

To slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; to disbelieve in cause and effect—these constitute the immediate offenses (*ānantarya-karma*). One should always know that when a person dies, they undergo rebirth according to the law of retribution.

One should always know how to distance oneself from evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends. One should always know that consulting and receiving teachings from the ninety-six kinds of heterodox masters is impermanent.

One should know that the three outflows (*āsrava*), the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are obstacles. One should always know the three miserable realms (*durgati*).
This is the place of the terrifying and most severe retributions of birth and death.

May I always know that in the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī, amidst the ocean-like assembly of beings, there is no sense of "mine," no mind of defiled attachment, no mind of anger or resentment, and no mind of weariness or indolence;

rather, may I possess a superior mind, a profound mind, a concentrated mind, and a mind that delights in the Dharma—a mind that extinguishes all afflictions and departs from the evil realms—and may I always know all things.
The practices of the Bodhisattvas are fully accomplished with immeasurable merit; they have attained profound meditative concentration and perfected the mind of the One Vehicle.
Having already resolved their will and fulfilled their vows, they together, with sincere hearts, prostrate themselves on the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

One does not allow evil to result in bitter fruit. One does not say that when a person dies there is annihilation and no further rebirth. One does not speak of matters that are useless or harmful to others.
One does not speak of the scriptures composed by non-Buddhists. One does not teach people to commit the ten unwholesome actions.

The Buddha granted him a prophecy. Chapter Nine: The Practice for Seeking Rebirth As for the practice for seeking rebirth, there are five gates of mindfulness and four directions of cultivation. Here, one’s pure karma (*śukla-karman*) ripens for that land where the red lotus has already blossomed.

Considering the capacities of those who are sharp or dull, and extensively explaining the teachings of sudden and gradual, one should first cultivate progress according to one’s strength, weighing one’s own efforts. Taking advantage of leisure time and selecting a secluded place, one may follow the track of the nine grades, or rely on the regulations of the three classes. Alternatively, one may form a society based on favorable conditions, or...

Without a superior companion, one must practice in solitude; however, one should seek like-minded associates to deeply investigate the Buddha Vehicle. Do not engage in idle talk with others regarding worldly affairs; rather, you should strictly cut off social interactions and cast aside mundane attachments. Speak nothing that is meaningless, and do not go forth at improper times.

Wearing simple robes and eating plain vegetarian food, protect the precepts and observe the fasts. Dedicate your practice and vows toward the Western Land; through the dedicated cultivation of its principles and phenomena, you will certainly attain rebirth there. If you rely on this method, you will surely achieve rebirth in Jambudvīpa within a short time, and enjoy the leisure of Sukhāvatī for immeasurable kalpas.
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice has together completed the initiation of the great vow for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Next, you should gradually rely upon the practices for seeking birth and cultivate progress in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore, if one possesses the vow but lacks the practice, that vow will surely be empty.
If one practices without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary. It is essential that practice and aspiration correspond, and that merit and wisdom support one another;

only then will one certainly attain rebirth and swiftly accomplish the holy path. With sincere devotion, prostrate yourself with your five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Now, having compiled various practices from the various sutras, I respectfully urge each person to do so.
Whether following the extensive or concise versions, practicing according to the sutras will ensure that one attains the supreme fruit in its entirety. The verse says:
At the time of morning each day when first beginning practice, Join the palms facing west and recite the holy name ten times;
Then perform prostrations once more. This is as explained within the *Longshu Jingtu Wen* (The Text on the Pure Land by Longshu).

*The Brief Diagram of the Swift Path for Textual Liberation from Saṃsāra by Longshu Wen Chao* states: Over ten scriptures in the Great Canon speak of the matters of the Western Pure Land. All people are born within lotus flowers; food and clothing appear through transformation; they enjoy longevity without aging.

There are nine grades of dharma-gates for their practice. Now, I shall excerpt that which is accessible for the general public. It is said that Amitābha Buddha made this great vow: "When I become a Buddha, if sentient beings of the ten directions, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land..."

If, after reciting my name ten times, one does not attain rebirth [in my land], may I not become a Buddha. In this present life, it can eliminate calamities, resolve enmity, increase merit, and preserve longevity. Every morning, join your palms, face west, and prostrate, reciting: "Namo Amitābha Buddha; Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;

Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; Namo the Pure Ocean-like Assembly of Bodhisattvas. This concludes the ten recitations of the names. Prostrate once more. Next, recite the "Praise of the Buddha by the Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva" once, followed by the confession of sins, the dedication of merit, and the making of vows.

(The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost; delivering sentient beings through the nine grades, their majestic virtue is infinite. I now take great refuge and repent for the sins of the three karmas. Whatever merits and virtues exist, I wholeheartedly dedicate them.

May all those who recite the Buddha’s name be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of this life; may they behold the Buddha, resolve birth and death, and like the Buddha, deliver all beings.

(Then prostrate once more and withdraw. This verse possesses great power; it can extinguish all sins and increase all blessings. To teach others to recite [the Buddha's name] brings such merit and reward. If one is thus truly sincere, one will certainly be reborn in the Middle Grade. If one further adds diligence, it will transform...)

If one transforms others and causes them to encourage and transform one another, one will be reborn in the superior grade. Even if a person of evil deeds practices this, they will still be reborn in the lower grade. By recollecting the Buddha here in this world, a single lotus flower will grow in a pond of seven treasures in the Western Land, bearing one's name;

on another day, one will take rebirth within it. This is vastly different from having one’s name recorded in the underworld, where one awaits the arrival of messengers to summon one when one’s life has ended.
Today, you members of this assembly gathered at the site of practice, must well restrain your minds and ears; listen with longing and attentiveness. The Treatise by Vasubandhu states:
"If there are those who wish to be born in that land, they should be encouraged to cultivate the five gates of mindfulness. If these five gates are complete, one will certainly attain birth there."

What are these five? First is the gate of physical action through prostration. This means to single-mindedly and resolutely pay homage to that Amitābha Buddha with reverent palms joined and offerings of incense and flowers;
"prostration" here refers specifically to prostrating before that Buddha alone, vowing to do so until the end of one's life without intermingling it with other forms of worship.
Second is the gate of verbal action through praise, which means to praise with focused intent.
This is because of the radiance of that Buddha’s physical marks, the radiance of the individual marks of all the holy assembly, and the radiance of all the jewel-adornments within that land.
Third is the gate of mental activity consisting of contemplative observation:
namely, to single-mindedly contemplate the physical marks, radiance, and the adornments of the land of that Buddha and the entire holy assembly, as one would practice visualization.
The Sūtra states: "Except for the time of sleep, one should always remember, always keep in mind, always contemplate, and always observe this matter.

Fourth is the gate of making vows: that is to say, with single-minded devotion, whether by day or by night, at all times and in all places, regarding the merit performed through the three karmas and four modes of conduct, regardless of whether it is the beginning, middle, or end, one must always make a vow from within a sincere heart, vowing to be reborn...

Because of that land. Fifth is the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This refers to single-mindedly performing roots of goodness oneself, and deeply giving rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) for all the roots of goodness performed by each and every ordinary being and sage throughout the three vehicles and five destinies—just as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to sympathetic joy, so too do I give rise to sympathetic joy.
By means of these roots of goodness from sympathetic joy, as well as those of my own...
They cultivate roots of goodness and share them all with sentient beings, dedicating them toward that land.

Having arrived in that land, they attain the six supernormal powers and enter the cycle of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings until the end of time, their minds never weary or satisfied.
This continues until the attainment of Buddhahood; it is also called the gate of dedication. Once these five gates are complete, one will certainly attain rebirth.
Whatever karmic practices one undertakes, regardless of their quantity, are all termed "genuine karma."

The *Daqin lun* (Treatise on Great Kindness) states: "By practicing the four methods of cultivation through contemplation, employing the three types of mental resolve, and performing the practice of the five recollections, one will swiftly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. What are these four? First is 'cultivation through reverence. Because one reverently prostrates before that Buddha and all the holy assembly, it is called cultivation through reverence.

One vows not to stop until the end of life; this is cultivation at all times, which accords with the *Ganlu shu* (Commentary on the Nectar). The *Shu* says: 'Cultivation through reverence also has five aspects. First, regarding the Principal Saint who is one's karmic connection, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down...'"

Furthermore, even those who have committed impurities and defilements shall all attain rebirth in the Western Land. Second, one should revere those with whom there is a karmic affinity for the Image-Teaching (the Mahāyāna): by setting up images of Amitābha and upholding his teachings. Third, one should revere teachers and friends with whom there is a karmic affinity: because of revering and drawing near to them.

Fourth, one should revere fellow students—that is, those who practice the Pure Land path together—because they mutually exhort and benefit one another. Fifth, one must always revere the Triple Gem, as it is the supreme condition for birth there. By practicing with such reverence, one will certainly attain rebirth. Second is "exclusive cultivation," which means single-mindedly reciting the name of that Buddha.

To focus one's thoughts and offer prostrations exclusively, praising that Buddha and the entire assembly of noble ones without intermingling other activities, is therefore called "unmixed cultivation" (*anavaśeṣa-bhāvanā*). To take the end of one's life as the limit and vow not to desist is what constitutes "cultivation at all times" (*nitya-kāla-bhāvanā*). Third is "uninterrupted cultivation" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).

What is called "continuous practice" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*) refers to the uninterrupted succession of reverent prostrations, reciting names, praising, mindfulness, contemplation, dedication, and making vows. Because these mental states follow one another without being interrupted by other activities, it is called continuous practice.

Furthermore, because it is not interrupted by afflictions such as greed or anger—confessing immediately upon transgression so that no thought-moment, period of time, or day is left unpurified—it is also called continuous practice. To take the end of one's life as the limit and vow never to cease is what constitutes "constant-time practice. Fourth is "dedication practice":

this means that once a Bodhisattva has escaped birth and death, they dedicate all the wholesome dharmas they have performed toward seeking the fruit of Buddhahood; this is self-benefit. To teach and transform sentient beings until the end of the future is altruistic benefit. However, at present, sentient beings...

Bound by afflictions, one has not yet escaped the sufferings of the evil realms, birth and death, and so forth. As one’s actions arise according to conditions, quickly redirect all roots of goodness toward the aspiration to be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha. Once you have reached that land, there will be nothing further to fear.
Through these four practices mentioned above, self-benefit and benefit for others will naturally and spontaneously be fully perfected.
The Gate of Seeking Rebirth through the Samādhi of One Practice: Dwelling alone in a quiet, secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts;
bind the mind in single-minded recollection and behold Amitābha. As stated in the Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra:

"If one wishes to clarify the Samādhi of One Practice, one should only be exhorted to dwell alone in a quiet, secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and bind the mind to a single Buddha. Without contemplating physical marks, focus exclusively on reciting the name; then, within that very recollection, one shall behold him."

"Amitābha Buddha and all other Buddhas alike. Question: For what reason do they not instruct one to practice visualization (*vipaśyanā*), but instead directly dispatch one to exclusively recite the Name? Answer: It is because sentient beings may have heavy karmic obstructions, making visualization difficult to accomplish. For this reason, the Great Sage, out of compassionate pity, directly exhorts exclusive recitation of the Name.

This is precisely because reciting the Name is easy, and thus [the practice] can continue uninterruptedly. Question: When one exclusively recites the name of a single Buddha, why do many appear? Is this not a case of the intermingling of the heterodox and the orthodox, where the one and the many manifest together? Answer: Because the great compassion of all Buddhas is equal, and because Amitābha’s power of vows is profound. Question:

Since all Buddhas equally realize the three bodies (*trikāya*), and their fruition of compassion and wisdom is perfected, they should likewise be non-dual. When one pays homage and mindfulness according to one's direction, and performs the prescribed recitations...

One might ask: "Since one Buddha should likewise be able to grant birth [in his land], for what reason do you exclusively praise the West? What is the significance of focusing specifically on prostration, mindfulness, and so forth? The answer is: "That which all Buddhas realize is equal and one. However, when considered in terms of their practices and vows, there are certainly causes and conditions."

However, the World-Honored One Amitābha originally made profound and solemn vows, vowing to gather and transform beings throughout the ten directions by means of his radiant light and name. Provided that one seeks him with faith and mindfulness—whether for the duration of one's entire life, or down to ten recitations, or even a single recitation—one will easily attain rebirth through the power of the Buddha’s vow.

For this reason, Śākyamuni and all other Buddhas exhort [beings] toward the Western Quarter; it is merely a matter of distinction. It is certainly not the case that invoking and reciting the names of other Buddhas cannot eliminate obstacles or extinguish transgressions.

Observe and visualize Amitābha Buddha, And the two Great Beings, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Being born in the Pure Land seated upon lotus flowers; Thus it is taught in the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*.

(The Brief Method for Cultivation and Practice of the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations* states: Having purified oneself through fasting and precepts, with a clear mind and pure thoughts, sit facing west in a composed posture. Close your eyes and remain silent. Visualize the true golden-colored body of Amitābha Buddha, located seven [palms] to the west...)

He sits upon a great lotus flower in the midst of a jewel pond. His body is sixteen feet tall. Between his two eyebrows, there is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) that curls upward to the right, its radiance shining brilliantly. His body is the color of purple gold.

By settling the mind and focusing one’s thoughts upon this white tuft of hair, one must not allow even a fraction of a thought of anything else to arise; one should do this whether the eyes are closed or open, so that he is seen in every instance. This is intended to ensure that mindfulness is never distracted from moment to moment. After practicing in this way for a long time, when the mind of recollection has matured, there will naturally be a response, and one will see the Buddha’s entire body.

This method is the most supreme; it is said that when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this very mind is itself the Buddha. Furthermore, it surpasses oral recitation. Next, visualize the body of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara as being the color of purple gold, with a white lotus flower in his palm.

Within his celestial crown is a standing transformation Buddha. Next, visualize the body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta as purple-gold in color; upon his celestial crown and usnīṣa is a precious vase.

Next, visualize yourself being born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower. Form the visualization of the lotus petals closing, and then the visualization of them opening to see Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the entirety of space.
Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this place of practice, listen with sincere hearts. The *Commentary on the Scripture of the Receptive Acceptance of Praise for the Pure Land* states:
"There are two aspects to the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recollection: namely, mind and mouth. Mind constitutes the essence of recollection; mouth constitutes the manifestation of recollection."

Mental recitation is profound and difficult; oral recitation is shallow and easy. Both are the primary practices for rebirth in the Western Land, as they correspond to the varying capacities of practitioners, which range from superior to inferior.
Now, I shall briefly set forth the methods for mental and oral recitation, dividing them into two sections.

Furthermore, regarding mental recollection: in a quiet place, throughout the six periods of the day, after completing the offerings, prostrations, praises, and the practice of the path, one emerges from the maṇḍala and arrives at one's dwelling.
Whether sitting or standing, if one wishes to enter into the contemplation of the Buddha, one should do so.

Facing west, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, recite ten times the names of the Great Compassionate Ones—Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

Having done so, make this vow: "I, your disciple, am currently an ordinary person in the cycle of birth and death, burdened by deep and heavy karmic obstacles, wandering through the six realms of existence beyond description.
Today, having encountered a true spiritual friend, I have been able to hear [the name of the Buddha]..."

Although one may recite the name of Amitābha Buddha’s original vow in the hope of attaining rebirth in his land, how can one do so while remaining ignorant of the physical marks, radiance, and features of Amitābha Buddha, as well as those of the two great Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta?

I pray that the Buddha will not forsake his great original vow of universal salvation, but out of compassion will receive me and cause me, his disciple, to behold them. Even when lying down to sleep, I shall likewise make this vow. And so it was.
In dreams, one may at times behold them.
Today, this assembly of fellow practitioners at the site of enlightenment shall, for the sake of all who seek rebirth, together direct their sincere minds toward this end.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, I take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

The Gate of Seeking Birth through the Three Grades:
Abandoning home and renouncing attachments to become a śramaṇa, one awakens the bodhicitta and cultivates merit;
the Buddha and his great assembly then appear before them, and they immediately attain birth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Ānanda, "Among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, those who possess a sincere heart and aspire to be born in that land are divided into three classes. As for those of the highest class, they renounce their homes and abandon desire to become śramaṇas."

Having resolved to attain Bodhicitta, one should single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha, cultivate various meritorious virtues, and vow to be born in that land. At the time of death, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before that person; thereupon, one shall follow that Buddha.

Upon being reborn in that land, one will be spontaneously born by transformation amidst flowers made of the seven treasures, dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, possessing courageous wisdom and mastery of supernatural powers.

Therefore, Ānanda, any sentient beings who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha in this present life should cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues with the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi, vowing to be born in that land.

Cultivating goodness according to conditions and observing the fasts and precepts, hanging silk banners, scattering flowers, and burning lamps and incense, one’s body will follow the transformation-buddhas to be born in that land; dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression, as described for those of the superior grade.

(The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for those of the middle grade, among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who possess a sincere resolve to be born in that land, though they cannot become śramaṇas or extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, they shall give rise to the aspiration for supreme bodhi...")

They shall fix their minds upon it, single-mindedly and exclusively mindful of Amitāyus Buddha. To whatever extent they cultivate goodness, uphold the precepts and fasts, erect stupas and images, provide food for śramaṇas, hang paintings, light lamps, scatter flowers, and burn incense—dedicating these merits with the vow to be born in that land—when such persons approach the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha will manifest a transformed body, possessing radiance and marks of excellence just like those of the true Buddha. Together with a great assembly, he will appear before them;
they will then follow this manifested Buddha and be reborn in that land, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression, with merit and wisdom equal to those of the superior grade.

If a person recites the name ten times or even once, with joyful faith and without doubt, they will see the Buddha in a dream at the time of death and attain rebirth; their merit is next only to that of the middle grade.

(The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for those of the lower grade, among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, if there are those who possess a resolute mind and desire to be born in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.")

If one directs one’s mind single-mindedly, even for ten recitations, to mindfulness of Amitāyus Buddha, vowing to be born in his land; or if, upon hearing the profound Dharma, one rejoices with faith and delight, giving rise to no doubt or confusion, and for even a single thought-moment mindfully recollects that Buddha with a heart of sincere resolve, vowing to be born in his land—such a person, at the time of death, will see that Buddha in a dream and shall likewise attain rebirth there. Their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the middle grade.

Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice, following the teachings of the Buddha as set forth in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, shall together cultivate the three grades of aspirants for the practice of seeking rebirth.
With single-minded resolve, we prostrate ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
